Real coordinates make geometric distances visible, and the complex arithmetic determines how polynomial maps transform those points. The complex plane is distinct from the Riemann sphere, which adds a point at infinity.

compression.label: compression
compression.preview: Compression reduces the amount of information needed to store, transmit, or read something.
compression.card: In Plectis's navigation, it means producing a shorter view of source material under rules about what must be preserved. The view keeps a route to the fuller source and makes important omissions or limits recoverable.
compression.rule: This use allows deliberate loss of detail, so preserving meaning requires judgement and checks.
compression.deep: A glossary preview, for example, should retain the defining idea while leaving examples and qualifications to the expanded entry.

compression_profile.label: compression profile
compression_profile.preview: A compression profile specifies how one kind of material should be presented at different levels of detail.
compression_profile.card: It defines what a short view must include, what it may omit, and how it links to the fuller account. Plectis uses profiles to make summaries of the same artifact kind follow consistent expectations.
compression_profile.rule: The profile governs the shape of a summary; the source governs its facts.
compression_profile.deep: For example, a result card may always need its claim and evidence status even when a very short version leaves out the supporting calculation.

computer_science.label: computer science
computer_science.preview: Computer science is the study of computation, algorithms, information, and the systems that process them.
computer_science.card: It includes theoretical questions about what can be computed as well as practical questions about languages, software, hardware, and reliable execution. CS is the usual abbreviation.
computer_science.rule: Formal verification is one part of this wider field.
computer_science.deep: On this site, computer-science contributions may concern the architecture, tools, checks, or reproducibility of the research workflow. They can improve how the mathematical work is produced and examined without themselves proving a mathematical claim.

concept.label: concept
concept.preview: A concept is an idea or category used to understand and organise a subject.
concept.card: Plectis also uses Concept as a structured record type: a recurring idea receives a stable identifier, definition, sources, and relationships. Other records can then refer to it consistently.
concept.rule: The record explains what the idea denotes; procedures describe how to act on it.
concept.deep: This separation helps detect vocabulary drift. If two mechanisms use the same name for different things, their shared concept reference provides a place to examine and resolve the mismatch.

concurrency.label: concurrency
concurrency.preview: Concurrency is the organization of multiple tasks whose execution or waiting periods overlap.
concurrency.card: Concurrent tasks can interleave on one processor or execute simultaneously on several processors. When they share mutable state or limited resources, their possible orderings require explicit coordination.
concurrency.rule: Concurrency permits overlapping progress but does not imply simultaneous execution; correctness depends on how shared state, ordering, cancellation, failures, and resource limits are coordinated.
concurrency.deep: Concurrency allows more than one task to be in progress during the same interval. A scheduler may interleave them on one processing unit, or hardware may run them in parallel. Overlap can improve responsiveness and resource use when one task waits for input or a service. It also creates several hazards: races depend on timing, deadlocks leave tasks waiting on one another, duplicate work can violate uniqueness assumptions, and concurrent writes can lose updates. Locks, transactions, message passing, immutable data, and ownership rules are different ways to control those interactions.

conditional_reduction.label: conditional reduction
conditional_reduction.preview: A conditional reduction proves that a target statement follows if a specified further condition holds.
conditional_reduction.card: The implication can be a complete theorem even while the condition remains unresolved. The reduction is useful when it exposes a more tractable question or clarifies exactly what additional evidence is needed.
conditional_reduction.rule: The target is still open until the required condition is established or another proof is found.
conditional_reduction.deep: A one-way implication need not give an equivalent problem. The new condition may be stronger than the target, so its difficulty and plausibility need separate assessment.

conditional_theorem.label: conditional theorem
conditional_theorem.preview: A conditional theorem proves a conclusion under stated hypotheses.
conditional_theorem.card: Mathematical theorems commonly have hypotheses. Here the label is especially useful when an important hypothesis remains unproved, so the theorem establishes an implication without yet establishing the desired conclusion on its own.
conditional_theorem.rule: Read the assumptions together with the conclusion, including assumptions supplied as parameters in Lean.
conditional_theorem.deep: A checked proof of “if H, then C” can be fully valid while H and C remain open. It is different from a proof containing an admitted step.

conformal_map.label: conformal map
conformal_map.preview: A conformal map preserves angles locally; in planar complex analysis, it is a holomorphic map with nonzero derivative.
conformal_map.card: A conformal map locally acts like a rotation and a positive scaling, with the scale allowed to vary between points. For example, z ↦ z² is conformal away from zero. It preserves local angles but can change lengths and areas.
conformal_map.rule: For planar complex domains verify that the map is holomorphic and has nonzero derivative; global one-to-one correspondence additionally requires injectivity and is not part of local conformality alone.
conformal_map.deep: A conformal map preserves oriented angles between intersecting curves at every point. For maps between open subsets of the complex plane, a holomorphic function is conformal wherever its derivative is nonzero. Such a map may stretch lengths and areas, but infinitesimally it acts as a rotation followed by a positive scaling. A conformal bijection has a conformal inverse and gives an equivalence of domains. A Riemann map is a special conformal bijection between a proper simply connected planar domain and the unit disc, so conformal map and Riemann map are not interchangeable names.

congruence.label: congruence
congruence.preview: Two integers are congruent modulo m if their difference is divisible by m.
congruence.card: For a positive modulus, this is equivalent to having the same remainder. Thus 17 ≡ 2 modulo 5 because 17 − 2 = 15 is divisible by 5.
congruence.rule: Congruence is weaker than equality: infinitely many different integers can be congruent to one another.
congruence.deep: The papers use congruences to keep only the remainder information relevant to an argument. A nonzero remainder can rule out divisibility even when the original expression is too large to inspect directly.

conjecture.label: conjecture
conjecture.preview: A conjecture is a precise mathematical claim proposed as true but not yet established by proof.
conjecture.card: Examples, calculations, and partial results may make a conjecture plausible. A proof must cover its full statement; a counterexample must satisfy its hypotheses while violating its conclusion.
conjecture.rule: Evidence from many cases does not by itself settle a claim about all cases.
conjecture.deep: The papers can give equivalent formulations or sufficient conditions for a conjecture. Those are useful results, but the conjecture stays unresolved unless the additional work actually establishes or refutes it.

connected_component.label: connected component
connected_component.preview: A connected component is a connected subset that cannot be enlarged while remaining connected within the surrounding space.
connected_component.card: Connected means that the part cannot be separated into two disjoint, nonempty relatively open pieces. Each point belongs to exactly one connected component.
connected_component.rule: Connectedness need not provide a continuous path between every pair of points in an arbitrary space.
connected_component.deep: In the lemniscate papers, components distinguish separate regions around polynomial roots. Statements requiring an actual path or a length bound need more than merely identifying which connected component contains a point.

connected_set.label: connected set
connected_set.preview: A set that cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open pieces relative to that set.
connected_set.card: An interval is connected, while two separated intervals are not. Connectedness says the set is one topological piece even when no particular path has yet been supplied.
connected_set.rule: Path connected implies connected, but the converse can fail in general spaces. Do not silently replace a connected-set claim by a stronger path claim.
connected_set.deep: The lower-bound argument applies to every connected set containing two selected roots, so it is stronger than checking only straight segments or one chosen curve.

context_packet.label: context packet
context_packet.preview: A context packet is a selected collection of information supplied for a particular task.
context_packet.card: Plectis uses packets to give an agent the relevant question, source routes, constraints, and current evidence without requiring it to read the whole repository. Public reader packets serve a similar orientation purpose.
context_packet.rule: A packet should make its scope and source versions clear.
context_packet.deep: Selection necessarily leaves things out. Links to the underlying material let a reader recover missing detail and check whether a summary still agrees with the sources it describes.

context_window.label: context window
context_window.preview: A context window is the bounded sequence of tokens a language model can use during a generation.
context_window.card: The window can contain instructions, conversation, retrieved documents, tool results, and tokens generated so far. These compete for finite space, although input and output limits vary by model. Token capacity measures available context, not comprehension, permanent memory, or factual reliability.
context_window.rule: A larger window permits more input but does not guarantee that every included detail is used accurately or with equal attention.
context_window.deep: A context window bounds the tokens a language model can directly condition on for one generation. Instructions, conversation, retrieved passages, tool results, and the requested output budget all consume capacity. Content outside that window has no direct effect unless another mechanism retrieves or summarizes it back in. Large capacity does not create durable memory, guarantee recall, or ensure equal attention across positions. Tokenization also means character count and word count do not map uniformly to available space, especially across code, mathematics, and languages.

continuous_integration.label: continuous integration
continuous_integration.preview: Continuous integration is the practice of frequently combining code changes and automatically checking that they work together.
continuous_integration.card: A CI service reacts to selected repository changes by running declared builds, tests, linters, or policy checks in a controlled environment. It gives collaborators evidence about whether changes integrate and preserves logs and status. The result covers the configured jobs and their environment.
continuous_integration.rule: A green CI result means the configured checks passed for that revision; it is not proof of correctness, security, deployability, or review.
continuous_integration.deep: Continuous integration combines small repository changes frequently and runs declared automation against each selected revision. Typical jobs compile code, execute tests, check formatting, scan dependencies, or build documentation in a controlled environment. The practice detects integration faults early and leaves reviewable logs, but its authority ends at configured checks, fixtures, platforms, and permissions. A green result establishes only what the completed checks justify; a skipped job or an untested requirement is not covered by the colour of the overall status. Reproducibility also depends on pinned dependencies and a faithfully described runner environment.

contradiction.label: contradiction
contradiction.preview: A contradiction is an impossibility obtained from assumptions, such as a statement and its negation both being true.
contradiction.card: In proof by contradiction, one assumes the opposite of the desired conclusion and derives such an impossibility. Classical reasoning then rules out that opposite assumption.
contradiction.rule: Each inference must follow from the assumptions actually available at that point.
contradiction.deep: For example, an irrationality argument may assume a number equals a fraction in lowest terms, then show both numerator and denominator must share a factor. That conflicts with the lowest-terms assumption.

contrapositive.label: contrapositive
contrapositive.preview: In classical logic, the contrapositive of “if P, then Q” is the equivalent statement “if not Q, then not P”.
contrapositive.card: For example, “every multiple of 4 is even” gives “an odd integer is not a multiple of 4”. Either version expresses the same implication through a different route.
contrapositive.rule: The converse, “if Q, then P”, is a different statement and need not hold.
contrapositive.deep: The papers often prove that rationality would force a property, then establish failure of that property to deduce irrationality. The reasoning must negate the exact consequence, with its quantifiers intact.

contribute.label: contribute
contribute.preview: To contribute is to supply work that helps a shared project advance or correct itself.
contribute.card: Here useful contributions include proofs, counterexamples, clearer explanations, software fixes, and reproducible reports of failed approaches. The public repositories provide concrete material against which a contribution can be inspected.
contribute.rule: Acceptance and attribution should follow the work and evidence, not the confidence of its presentation.
contribute.deep: A mathematical result remains attributable to the people who established it. Using Plectis as a tool or starting point does not transfer priority for their result to the project.

contributor_credit.label: contributor credit
contributor_credit.preview: Contributor credit records who supplied a piece of work and what that contribution was.
contributor_credit.card: Plectis aims to preserve attribution for accepted results, corrections, and other useful work, including when later work builds on them. Describing the contribution makes the credit more informative than simply listing a name.
contributor_credit.rule: Human authorship and the use of AI or other tools should be recorded distinctly.
contributor_credit.deep: The project's contribution record is not a substitute for scholarly priority or publication conventions. A result's authors retain credit for establishing it, including when this system helped them work.

convergence.label: convergence
convergence.preview: Convergence means approaching a specified limit; for an infinite series, it means that its partial sums approach a finite value.
convergence.card: For a real sequence, every chosen positive tolerance must eventually contain all later terms around the limit. For a series, apply that condition to the sums of the first n terms.
convergence.rule: Terms tending to zero are necessary for a series to converge, but are not sufficient.
convergence.deep: For example, 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ diverges. Proving convergence also leaves separate questions about whether the sum is rational, algebraic, or transcendental.

convex_combination.label: convex combination
convex_combination.preview: A weighted sum whose weights are nonnegative and add to one.
convex_combination.card: One quarter of x plus three quarters of y lies on the line segment between x and y.
convex_combination.rule: Allowing negative weights while keeping their total equal to one gives an affine combination. A general linear combination need not have weights summing to one.
convex_combination.deep: The trinomial root equation places normalized polynomial values inside the convex hull of two controlled quantities.

coprime.label: coprime
coprime.preview: Two integers are coprime if their greatest common divisor is 1.
coprime.card: They have no positive common divisor other than 1, or equivalently no common prime factor. For example, 8 and 15 are coprime even though neither is prime.
coprime.rule: A fraction is in lowest terms when its numerator and denominator are coprime.
coprime.deep: In modular arithmetic, an integer has a multiplicative inverse modulo m exactly when it is coprime to m. This is why coprimality often appears among the hypotheses of statements about multiplicative order.

corpus.label: corpus
corpus.preview: A corpus is a collection of material studied or managed as a body of work.
corpus.card: The site uses the term for collections such as formal declarations, papers, or recorded examples. A particular revision or manifest can fix which items belong to the collection being described.
corpus.rule: Any reported count or check should identify the corpus and version it covers.
corpus.deep: A corpus can grow or change over time. Results about one snapshot should not silently be treated as results about every later version or every related repository.

counterexample.label: counterexample
counterexample.preview: A counterexample is a case that satisfies a claim's assumptions but makes its conclusion false.
counterexample.card: One counterexample disproves a universal statement. For instance, 2 is a counterexample to “every prime number is odd”, because it is prime and even.
counterexample.rule: An example outside the assumptions does not refute the statement.
counterexample.deep: Counterexamples in the working records may target an attempted lemma or method rather than the original open problem. Naming the exact statement they refute preserves that distinction and explains what a revised approach must avoid.

coverage.label: coverage
coverage.preview: Coverage is the measured portion of a declared population, requirement set, behavior space, or source surface that has been examined or represented.
coverage.card: The denominator and matching method determine what the number means. Test coverage can report executed statements or branches; corpus coverage can report linked records; proof coverage can report which stated obligations have formal evidence. None of these automatically establishes correctness of covered items.
coverage.rule: Ask what total set was declared, how membership and matches were determined, when measurement occurred, and which uncovered cases remain.
coverage.deep: Coverage converts a bounded inventory into a numerator, denominator, and method. High test coverage can coexist with weak assertions or missing behaviors. Complete proof coverage may mean every declared obligation has a proof while the specification itself omits an important requirement. Source or documentation coverage can be exact within a known catalogue yet silent about objects outside it. Comparisons are meaningful only when inventories and methods align. A useful receipt therefore preserves the authority for the denominator, exclusions, measurement version, and concrete uncovered set.

critic_posture.label: critic posture
critic_posture.preview: Critic posture is a deliberate way of examining an idea for weaknesses before relying on it.
critic_posture.card: Plectis uses it to ask concrete questions: whether an abstraction fits the evidence, whether a proposed route can be executed, and whether a necessary rule or check is missing.
critic_posture.rule: A useful criticism identifies the affected claim and the evidence that would resolve it.
critic_posture.deep: This turns an objection into work that can be assessed. The critic's role is to test the idea, while any resulting change still needs an owner and validation.

critical_point.label: critical point
critical_point.preview: For a smooth real-valued function, a critical point is an input where all first partial derivatives vanish.
critical_point.card: For a complex polynomial p, a critical point c satisfies p′(c) = 0. For p(z) = z² − 1, the critical point is 0, whereas the roots are 1 and −1. In several real variables, all first partial derivatives must vanish together.
critical_point.rule: A critical point and a root need not be the same point.
critical_point.deep: Some elementary conventions also include points of nondifferentiability. The polynomial setting here is differentiable everywhere, and critical points matter because the Newton expression −p/p′ is undefined there.

critical_value.label: critical value
critical_value.preview: A critical value is the output of a function at one of its critical points.
critical_value.card: For p(z) = z² − 1, the critical point 0 has critical value −1. The point and value lie on different sides of the function: one is an input and the other is its image.
critical_value.rule: The modulus |p(c)| is the magnitude of a critical value, not the value itself.
critical_value.deep: The lemniscate arguments compare these magnitudes and directions to study how regions can meet. Distinct critical points can share a critical value, and different values can have the same magnitude.

curve_parametrisation.label: curve parametrisation
curve_parametrisation.preview: A function from a parameter interval into a space whose image traces a curve.
curve_parametrisation.card: The map t ↦ (cos t,sin t), for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, traces the unit circle once counterclockwise. A parametrisation specifies a position for every parameter value, and a differentiable parametrisation also determines direction and speed.
curve_parametrisation.rule: Separate the parametrised map from its image: different parametrisations can trace the same geometric curve, with different speeds or orientations.
curve_parametrisation.deep: A parametrisation of a curve is a map gamma from an interval into a space, usually Euclidean or complex space. Its image is the geometric set traced by gamma. When gamma is differentiable, gamma'(t) gives velocity; if that derivative never vanishes, the parametrisation is regular. Replacing t by a suitable increasing function changes speed without changing orientation or image, while a decreasing replacement reverses orientation. Curve length is unchanged by sufficiently regular one-to-one reparametrisation, but a map that retraces part of the curve can count that part more than once.

field.label: data field
field.preview: A data field is a named part of a structured record that holds a value with an expected meaning and form.
field.card: A result record might have fields for its status, timestamp, and source revision. A schema states which fields are required, what values they accept, and how absence or an empty value is interpreted. This computing meaning differs from an algebraic field or a field of study.
field.rule: A field name identifies its role within a record or schema; the same name in another schema can have a different meaning.
field.deep: Fields let programs locate specific information without inferring it from free text. Their values can be numbers, strings, lists, nested records, or other allowed data. A missing field, an explicit null value, and an empty string may express different states. The site uses fields to preserve exact identifiers and checking results across generated views. Merely recording a value does not show that it is accurate, current, or supported by evidence; those properties require their own checks.

database.label: database
database.preview: A database is an organized collection of data maintained so it can be accessed, queried, and updated.
database.card: A relational database organizes records in tables; document, graph, and key-value databases use other models. A database management system provides the software for storing, querying, and changing those records. Everyday computing prose often uses “database” for both the data and that running service.
database.rule: Database behavior is defined by its data model, schema, query and update semantics, consistency, transactions, indexes, access controls, replication, and backup policy.
database.deep: A database is the organized data, managed through software often called a database management system; a dataset groups records for a particular analysis or other purpose. A query result may reflect one transaction snapshot, a replica lag, cached values, permissions, or later updates. Constraints can prevent some invalid states but cannot establish that recorded facts are true. Replication improves availability yet introduces consistency choices. Reliable interpretation names the database instance or export, schema version, query, time, and whether the result came from live, cached, replicated, or archived state.

dataset.label: dataset
dataset.preview: A dataset is an organized collection of observations or records intended to be considered together.
dataset.card: A table of measurements, labelled images, survey responses, documents, or synthetic examples can each be a dataset. Its meaning depends on what was collected, from whom, when, and how.
dataset.rule: A dataset is characterized by its population, sampling and collection process, fields, units, labels, exclusions, version, and known transformations.
dataset.deep: Datasets do not speak independently of their construction. Missing groups, duplicated records, measurement error, label ambiguity, selection bias, data leakage, later corrections, and incompatible versions can change an analysis. A dataset may be representative for one question and unsuitable for another. Synthetic data reflects assumptions of its generator rather than direct observation. Train, validation, and test partitions are roles assigned to records, not different kinds of evidence. Reproducible conclusions identify the exact version and preprocessing used.

declaration.label: declaration
declaration.preview: A declaration introduces a named item in a programming or proof language, such as a definition, theorem, or structure.
declaration.card: In Lean, the declaration's source states its type and, where applicable, its value or proof. Later declarations can use that name, creating a chain of dependencies.
declaration.rule: A declaration count combines different kinds of items and is not a count of distinct mathematical discoveries.
declaration.deep: To assess a theorem, inspect its exact statement, proof dependencies, and assumptions. Supporting definitions and routine lemmas may be necessary without being separate research contributions.

integral.label: definite integral
integral.preview: A definite integral accumulates a function’s values over a specified region using a rule for measuring that region.
integral.card: For example, integrating 2x from 0 to 1 gives 1, the area under that graph over the interval. Integrals can also describe mass, averages, energy, and curve length. Signed values can cancel, so an integral need not equal the total unsigned area.
integral.rule: Check the integration domain, variable, and notion of integration; finite Riemann integration and Lebesgue integration agree for continuous functions on compact intervals but have different general scope.
integral.deep: A definite integral combines the values of a function over a specified domain. The Riemann integral is built from limits of weighted sums over finer partitions and is well suited to bounded functions on finite intervals. The Lebesgue integral groups values using a measure and handles wider classes of functions and limit operations. Continuous functions on a closed bounded interval are integrable in both senses with the same value. An improper integral is a limit used for an unbounded domain or singular integrand, so convergence must be proved rather than assumed.

polynomial_degree.label: degree of a polynomial
polynomial_degree.preview: The degree of a nonzero polynomial is the highest exponent with a nonzero coefficient.
polynomial_degree.card: For example, 3z⁴ + 2z − 1 has degree 4, while a nonzero constant has degree 0. Over the complex numbers, a degree-n polynomial has n roots counted with multiplicity.
polynomial_degree.rule: The zero polynomial needs a separate degree convention because it has no nonzero coefficient.
polynomial_degree.deep: Degree constrains possible algebraic behaviour without determining the locations or distinctness of roots. The lemniscate papers use degree in quantitative estimates and sometimes prove results only for particular degree ranges.

demo_take.label: Demo Take
demo_take.preview: Demo Take is the system's recording tool for capturing a demonstration and its accompanying material.
demo_take.card: It brings screen recording, transcript capture, and still frames into one workflow. The resulting files can then support a prepared demonstration without reconstructing the session from separate recordings.
demo_take.rule: A recorded demonstration shows the particular run and material that were captured.
demo_take.deep: It is useful for explanation and review, while repeatability still depends on the source, inputs, environment, and commands behind what appears on screen.

denominator.label: denominator
denominator.preview: The denominator is the divisor in a fraction: the b in a/b, where b is nonzero.
denominator.card: In 3/4, the denominator is 4. For a positive fraction interpreted as equal-sized parts, it specifies that the whole has been divided into four parts.
denominator.rule: Cancelling a common factor changes the written denominator without changing the fraction's value.
denominator.deep: Number-theory arguments often require the denominator in lowest terms. For example, whether a fraction terminates in a chosen numeral base depends on the prime factors of that reduced denominator.

dense_subset.label: dense subset
dense_subset.preview: A subset whose closure is the whole surrounding space.
dense_subset.card: The rational numbers are dense in the real line: every open interval, however short, contains a rational. They still omit most real numbers, so dense does not mean equal to the surrounding space or large by counting.
dense_subset.rule: A subset is dense when its closure is the whole space, equivalently when every nonempty open region meets it. Density depends on the surrounding topology; changing the space can change the verdict.
dense_subset.deep: In the running-LCM paper, an irrational rotation has a dense orbit, allowing points arbitrarily close to any target location on the circle. Topological density concerns proximity, while asymptotic density concerns proportions of integers; any connection requires specifying the set and surrounding space.

dependency.label: dependency
dependency.preview: A dependency is an object, service, fact, or earlier result that another component or conclusion requires.
dependency.card: A software component may depend on a library, file, service, or build step; an argument may depend on a premise or earlier theorem. The dependency identifies a necessary input, not merely a related object.
dependency.rule: A dependency relation has a direction: the dependent item requires the upstream item, and a change or failure upstream can require downstream rebuilding, rechecking, or withdrawal.
dependency.deep: Dependencies connect work into a directed structure. In software, a package can require a particular library version, a generated file can require its source, and a service can require another service to answer. In reasoning, a conclusion depends on its premises and supporting results. Required dependencies prevent the dependent route from working when absent; optional dependencies affect only features that use them. Because changes can propagate downstream, dependency records often include versions, identities, and compatibility conditions. Cycles require special handling because no member can be prepared independently of the others.

deployment.label: deployment
deployment.preview: Deployment places a software version or configuration into an environment where it can run or serve users.
deployment.card: Building and testing an application creates candidate artifacts; deploying selects one and installs or activates it in development, staging, production, or another target environment.
deployment.rule: Deployment status identifies the artifact, target environment, configuration, rollout state, and whether traffic or users actually reach it.
deployment.deep: Deployment is distinct from committing source, merging a pull request, publishing a release, and proving that the service works correctly. A rollout may be partial, staged, paused, rolled back, or active only for selected users. Database migrations, secrets, feature flags, infrastructure, and cached assets can make two deployments of the same code behave differently. Successful deployment automation shows that its steps completed under defined checks; health monitoring and user-visible verification establish whether the deployed system remains available and behaves as intended.

derivation.label: derivation
derivation.preview: A derivation is a sequence of justified steps leading from stated starting points to a result.
derivation.card: In mathematics, the steps use definitions, assumptions, and valid inference rules. In the software descriptions, a derivation can instead describe how a generated object was obtained from its sources.
derivation.rule: The meaning of “justified” depends on the setting and the rules being used.
derivation.deep: Keeping the starting material and steps inspectable helps locate an error or repeat the process. A final answer alone may hide the assumption or transformation on which it depends.

derivation_certificate.label: derivation certificate
derivation_certificate.preview: A derivation certificate is an inspectable record that lets a checker verify how a particular claim follows from its stated basis.
derivation_certificate.card: Its form depends on the claim: it might be a formal proof object, a calculation trace, or structured data checked against source inputs. The checker must implement the connection between that record and the claimed result.
derivation_certificate.rule: Simply recording that a process ran does not certify every conclusion drawn from it.
derivation_certificate.deep: Plectis separates the producer, supporting record, and acceptance check so the basis for accepting a result can itself be examined.

derivative.label: derivative
derivative.preview: A derivative is the linear map that approximates a function's change to first order near a point.
derivative.card: For a function of one real or complex variable, the derivative at x is f′(x) = lim_{h→0}(f(x+h)−f(x))/h when this limit exists. For f(x) = x², expanding the quotient gives f′(x) = 2x. In several variables, the derivative acts on a direction of movement to give the corresponding first-order change.
derivative.rule: The approximation error must become negligible compared with the size of the input change. For complex functions, the difference quotient must approach the same limit from every complex direction.
derivative.deep: Polynomial critical points satisfy f'(c)=0, and the Newton vector field uses the quotient -f/f'.

determinant.label: determinant
determinant.preview: A determinant is a scalar computed from a square matrix; over a field, it is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible.
determinant.card: For the matrix with rows (a,b) and (c,d), its determinant is ad−bc. Over a field, a nonzero determinant means the matrix has an inverse. For real matrices, its absolute value gives the factor by which the map scales volume; its sign records orientation.
determinant.rule: A zero determinant signals dependence or collapse, but its numerical size depends on coordinate scaling.
determinant.deep: Plectis engineers evaluation matrices whose determinants are nonzero modulo selected primes, hence nonzero over the rationals.

deterministic.label: deterministic
deterministic.preview: A deterministic process produces the same output whenever all relevant inputs and operating conditions are the same.
deterministic.card: Determinism rules out unresolved random choice for a fixed execution state. Reproducibility still depends on treating versions, ordering, clocks, external responses, and configuration as inputs when they can affect the result.
deterministic.rule: The same specified input and environment determine one output; any random seed, time value, scheduling order, or external response that affects execution belongs among those conditions.
deterministic.deep: A deterministic algorithm maps each complete input state to one result. Running it twice with truly identical inputs therefore gives identical output. Apparent exceptions often come from hidden inputs: system time, directory order, concurrent scheduling, floating-point platform details, network responses, tool versions, or an unrecorded random seed. Determinism does not establish correctness, speed, or real-world validity; a consistently wrong calculation is still deterministic. It also differs from reproducibility, which asks whether another execution environment can reconstruct the conditions closely enough to obtain the recorded result.

diebold_mariano_test.label: Diebold-Mariano test
diebold_mariano_test.preview: The Diebold–Mariano test assesses whether two forecasting methods have equal expected loss under a chosen measure of error.
diebold_mariano_test.card: It compares the loss differences between paired forecasts and accounts for time dependence through an estimate of their long-run variance. Squared error and absolute error can lead to different comparisons.
diebold_mariano_test.rule: Interpret the result under the test's sampling and dependence assumptions.
diebold_mariano_test.deep: The test addresses average predictive loss in the analysed setting. Statistical significance neither identifies the cause of a difference nor guarantees that the better-performing method will remain better on future data.

differentiable_function.label: differentiable function
differentiable_function.preview: A function with a linear first-order approximation at each point under discussion.
differentiable_function.card: The derivative gives a linear approximation whose error becomes negligible compared with the change in input. Squaring is differentiable everywhere on the reals; absolute value is continuous at zero but has no derivative there because its two one-sided slopes disagree.
differentiable_function.rule: In several variables use the full linear approximation, not merely the existence of all partial derivatives; in complex analysis complex differentiability is substantially stronger than real differentiability.
differentiable_function.deep: For a real function of one variable, differentiability at x means that the difference quotient approaches a finite limit. In several real variables, differentiability means there is a linear map that approximates the increment with an error small compared with the increment's size. For a curve z(t), its derivative is its instantaneous velocity. For complex functions, the same quotient must have one limit independent of the direction of approach; differentiability on an open set then leads to holomorphicity. Differentiability implies continuity at the point, but continuity alone does not imply differentiability.

digest.label: digest
digest.preview: A cryptographic digest is a fixed-size value computed from data, used to detect whether the data has changed.
digest.card: The same bytes produce the same digest under the same algorithm. Plectis uses hashes to connect generated material and result records to particular file contents.
digest.rule: A mismatch proves the contents differ; a matching secure hash provides strong practical evidence of equality.
digest.deep: Different inputs can theoretically share a digest, so it is not a mathematical guarantee of identical bytes. A digest also says nothing about the truth or quality of the contents.

digestion.label: digestion
digestion.preview: Mathematical digestion is the process of understanding a result well enough to place it in the field and use it in further work.
digestion.card: It includes identifying the main idea, checking how the hypotheses matter, connecting the result to earlier work, and finding useful applications or reformulations. The site's discussion follows the distinction between verifying a proof and making its mathematics usable.
digestion.rule: A checked proof and a published paper can support this process without completing it.
digestion.deep: Clear explanations, failed approaches, and precise open questions help other mathematicians assess and continue the work. Community uptake cannot be awarded by a repository's own checks.

dimension.label: dimension
dimension.preview: A vector space has dimension equal to the size of a basis; geometric notions such as Hausdorff dimension use different definitions.
dimension.card: The ordinary plane has vector-space dimension two because every vector has a unique expression using two independent coordinate directions. A line through the origin has dimension one, while a space of all infinite sequences can be infinite-dimensional.
dimension.rule: Linear dimension is the size of a basis over a specified scalar field. Showing independent families of every finite size proves infinite-dimensionality. It does not mean each individual vector has infinitely many geometric directions.
dimension.deep: The arithmetic-function papers prove large or infinite linear dimension using evaluation matrices and independent channel families. Geometric notions such as Hausdorff dimension answer a different covering-scale question, so the qualifying word determines which definition applies.

dirichlet_convolution.label: dirichlet convolution
dirichlet_convolution.card: For arithmetic functions f and g, their Dirichlet convolution at a positive integer n is the sum of f(d)g(n/d) over positive divisors d of n. If both functions equal 1, the result counts divisors: for n = 6 it counts 1, 2, 3, and 6.
dirichlet_convolution.rule: The summation runs over divisors d of n and pairs each with n/d. This is not ordinary additive convolution, which sums over decompositions such as a+b=n. The identity element is 1 at n=1 and 0 elsewhere.
dirichlet_convolution.deep: Divisor transforms in the Mersenne and totient work reorganize coefficient sequences according to shared factors. Möbius inversion works because the Möbius function is the Dirichlet-convolution inverse of the constant-one function.

dirichlet_theorem_arithmetic_progression.label: dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
dirichlet_theorem_arithmetic_progression.preview: Dirichlet’s theorem says that every residue class a modulo a positive integer q with gcd(a,q) = 1 contains infinitely many primes.
dirichlet_theorem_arithmetic_progression.card: Dirichlet’s theorem guarantees infinitely many primes in every arithmetic progression a,a+q,a+2q,… when a and q are coprime. Thus both 1,5,9,… and 3,7,11,… contain infinitely many primes for modulus 4.
dirichlet_theorem_arithmetic_progression.rule: The coprimality condition gcd(a,q)=1 is essential. If a and q share a factor, every term shares it, so the progression contains at most one prime. The theorem asserts infinitude, not a specific first prime or short gap.
dirichlet_theorem_arithmetic_progression.deep: The totient construction uses this theorem to choose primes in engineered residue classes, making selected matrix entries nonzero while other entries gain prescribed factors. It is distinct from Dirichlet convolution and from other results bearing Dirichlet’s name.

discrete_mathematics.label: discrete mathematics
discrete_mathematics.preview: Discrete mathematics studies objects with separate elements, such as integers, graphs, and finite arrangements.
discrete_mathematics.card: Its questions include counting configurations, finding paths in networks, and proving properties of integer sequences. The objects may be finite or infinite; “discrete” does not mean “finite”.
discrete_mathematics.rule: The relevant structure is determined by the definitions of the problem.
discrete_mathematics.deep: Number theory and combinatorics supply many of the discrete methods used in these papers. Arguments may still involve continuous tools, such as real limits or analytic estimates, to study discrete objects.

distance.label: distance
distance.preview: A distance assigns zero to identical points, positive values to distinct points, and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality.
distance.card: On the real line, the distance from x to y is |x-y|; in the complex plane the same formula gives Euclidean distance. A valid distance is nonnegative, symmetric, and zero exactly when its two points coincide.
distance.rule: Distances obey d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z): traveling through y cannot beat the direct distance. A problem may use a different metric, such as hyperbolic distance, so always identify which distance is intended.
distance.deep: The lemniscate paper compares Euclidean separation, path length, and hyperbolic distance when selecting root connections. Two metrics can rank or scale pairs differently even on the same set; numerical bounds cannot be transferred without a proved comparison.

divergence.label: divergence
divergence.preview: A sequence or series diverges when it does not converge in the sense being considered.
divergence.card: For real sequences, failure to approach a finite limit can mean growing without bound or oscillating indefinitely. A series diverges when its sequence of partial sums fails to converge.
divergence.rule: Individual terms tending to zero do not ensure that their sum converges.
divergence.deep: The harmonic series is a standard example: its terms shrink to zero while its partial sums grow without bound. Papers should specify whether “diverges” means unbounded growth or another failure of convergence.

divisibility.label: divisibility
divisibility.preview: Divisibility is the relation in which one integer is an exact integer multiple of another.
divisibility.card: The notation a ∣ b means that b = ak for some integer k. For example, 3 divides 12 because 12 = 3·4, while 5 does not divide 12.
divisibility.rule: The direction matters: a ∣ b does not generally imply b ∣ a.
divisibility.deep: With this algebraic definition, every integer divides zero and zero divides only zero. The papers often impose positivity to exclude such cases, then use divisibility to track denominator cancellation, congruences, and prime factors.

divisor.label: divisor
divisor.preview: An integer d is a divisor of an integer n when n = d·k for some integer k.
divisor.card: For example, 3 divides 12 because 12 = 3·4. Number-theory statements usually specify positive divisors, while the divisibility relation itself can also involve negative integers or zero.
divisor.rule: The notation d ∣ n means “d divides n”.
divisor.deep: A divisor is an exact factor, so there is no remainder. With the stated algebraic definition, every integer divides zero, and zero divides only zero; additional positivity hypotheses often exclude these edge cases.

doctrine.label: doctrine
doctrine.preview: In Plectis, doctrine is the organised set of ideas and rules explaining how the system is intended to work.
doctrine.card: It includes principles, defined concepts, mechanisms, and guidance connected to source material. These records let agents recover the reasons behind an implementation rather than infer them from code alone.
doctrine.rule: A doctrine statement expresses a rule or interpretation; implementation evidence shows whether it is enacted.
doctrine.deep: Keeping the two connected makes disagreements visible. A rule can be clear while its software support is incomplete, or code can change while the explanation remains outdated.

doi.label: DOI
doi.preview: A DOI is a persistent identifier for an object such as a paper, dataset, or software release.
doi.card: It resolves through the DOI system to information maintained by the registering organisation. That destination can be updated when the object's web location changes, allowing the identifier to remain stable.
doi.rule: A DOI identifies material; it does not certify correctness, peer review, or permanence of access.
doi.deep: When citing work, use the DOI for the intended object or version. Different versions and related artifacts may have separate identifiers or explicit relationships in their metadata.

domain_expert.label: domain expert
domain_expert.preview: A domain expert is someone with substantial knowledge and judgement in a particular field.
domain_expert.card: For this project, relevant expertise may concern number theory, proof assistants, statistics, software architecture, or another subject addressed by a component. The useful expertise depends on the claim being examined.
domain_expert.rule: Expertise in one area does not automatically settle questions in another.
domain_expert.deep: An expert can help by assessing significance, detecting a missing assumption, relating a result to prior work, or explaining what would make the work easier for the field to use.

drift.label: drift
drift.preview: Drift is a mismatch that develops between things expected to agree, such as a generated page and its source.
drift.card: A source can change while a copied count, summary, or diagram continues to describe an older state. Plectis uses comparisons and refresh records to detect this kind of disagreement.
drift.rule: Identify the two objects, their versions, and the relationship being checked.
drift.deep: A drift report locates a mismatch; deciding which side needs correction requires knowing the authoritative source. Regenerating a page helps only if its builder is using the right inputs.

drilldown.label: drilldown
drilldown.preview: A drilldown opens a more detailed view of something shown in a summary.
drilldown.card: For example, a component count can lead to the component list, then to one component's source and recorded checks. Each step narrows the question and exposes more evidence.
drilldown.rule: The detailed view should preserve the identity of the item selected in the summary.
drilldown.deep: Plectis uses these routes to make a large system readable in stages. A summary remains useful when readers can recover the detail that was deliberately left out.

dyadic.label: dyadic
dyadic.preview: Dyadic means related to powers of two, often fractions or intervals built from them.
dyadic.card: A dyadic rational has the form m/2ⁿ for integers m and nonnegative n. Examples include 1/2, 3/8, and 5; each has a terminating binary expansion.
dyadic.rule: The exact object follows the noun: a dyadic interval or partition is not itself a number.
dyadic.deep: Dyadic scales are useful when repeatedly halving a range or relating binary digits to arithmetic. They provide a common structure for estimates, subdivisions, and expansions in base two.

empirical_distribution.label: empirical distribution
empirical_distribution.preview: An empirical distribution puts equal weight on each observation in a finite sample, adding weights when values repeat.
empirical_distribution.card: For observations 1,1,3, the empirical distribution places probability 2/3 on 1 and 1/3 on 3. Each observation receives equal weight before repeated values are combined, so the distribution summarizes observed frequencies.
empirical_distribution.rule: An empirical distribution comes from a finite sample. A limiting empirical distribution says these frequencies converge as sample size grows; it does not imply that observations are independent, random, or generated by that limiting law.
empirical_distribution.deep: The prime-gap countermodels preserve the empirical behavior detected by bounded short-block tests while altering the arithmetic conclusion of interest. This shows why matching many statistics can still fail to preserve denominator or irrationality structure.

endogenous.label: endogenous
endogenous.preview: Endogenous means originating within the system or process being discussed.
endogenous.card: An internal score, feedback signal, or judgement may be endogenous if the process being assessed also produces it. The term always depends on where the system boundary is drawn.
endogenous.rule: An internally produced measure can still be informative, but its dependencies matter.
endogenous.deep: In the site's research discussion, the concern is self-confirmation: repeated agreement among connected internal checks may provide less independent support than the number of agreeing outputs suggests.

engine_room.label: engine room
engine_room.preview: “Engine room” is the site's informal label for components that operate and maintain the system itself.
engine_room.card: These include routing, work queues, gates, and checks for mismatches between source and generated state. They support the workflow in which other components or mathematical work are developed.
engine_room.rule: The label groups a function within the architecture rather than naming a separate product.
engine_room.deep: An individual component in this group should still have a specific job, source, and evidence. The broad label alone does not explain what any particular mechanism has been shown to do.

entry.label: entry
entry.preview: In the navigation descriptions, an entry is either a starting route or an individual item in a collection.
entry.card: A command described as an entry route helps a reader choose the next relevant action. A glossary or catalog entry instead refers to one stored item with its own identity and detail.
entry.rule: The surrounding noun distinguishes these two common uses.
entry.deep: Plectis tries to make entry routes short enough for first contact while preserving links to the sources needed for the task. An entry should orient the reader before asking them to load deeper context.

environment.label: environment
environment.preview: An environment is the surrounding technical, physical, and procedural conditions under which work runs or an observation is made.
environment.card: In computing, an environment includes software, hardware, configuration, permissions, files, and services. In experimental work it also includes apparatus, physical conditions, sampling setting, and procedure. These surrounding conditions can change results even when the central instructions or source remain the same.
environment.rule: A result should identify the environmental conditions capable of affecting it, at the level of detail needed for reproduction or comparison.
environment.deep: Environment means the surrounding conditions under which an activity occurs, not only software configuration. For computation it can include operating system, hardware, runtime, libraries, variables, locale, clock, network, permissions, files, and external services. For experiments it also includes apparatus, physical conditions, sampling setting, and procedural controls. Build and runtime environments may differ. When results change, hidden environmental differences are plausible inputs rather than mere noise. Reproducibility requires recording the conditions capable of affecting the outcome at the precision relevant to the claim.

epistemic_control_plane.label: epistemic control plane
epistemic_control_plane.preview: The epistemic control plane is a proposed system layer that uses evidence and uncertainty to govern which actions may proceed.
epistemic_control_plane.card: “Epistemic” concerns what is known and how it is justified. The design connects a claim's evidence status to permitted actions, review requirements, and conditions that should stop a change.
epistemic_control_plane.rule: The phrase names a design target associated with the Workingness Instrument; the relevant implementation evidence must be checked separately.
epistemic_control_plane.deep: Its central idea is that changed evidence should change decisions. Recording uncertainty is useful only when the actions that depend on it respond appropriately.

equality.label: equality
equality.preview: An equality states that two expressions represent the same value or mathematical object.
equality.card: For example, 1/2 = 2/4 compares different expressions for the same number. Equality depends on the setting: two functions are equal when they agree as functions, not merely at a few tested inputs.
equality.rule: Distinguish equality from an approximation or a one-way implication.
equality.deep: In Lean, equality is itself a proposition that can require a proof. Two expressions that simplify to the same form may be equal for a more direct reason than expressions requiring a substantial theorem.

equation.label: equation
equation.preview: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal.
equation.card: It can specify a relation, define a quantity, or ask which values make the equality true. For example, x² = 4 has solutions x = 2 and x = −2 over the real numbers.
equation.rule: The permitted domain and assumptions determine what counts as a solution.
equation.deep: Some equations are identities that hold for every allowed value; others hold only for particular values. A displayed equality in a proof may express a justified transformation rather than a problem to solve.

equivalence.label: equivalence
equivalence.preview: Two statements are logically equivalent when each implies the other under the same assumptions.
equivalence.card: To establish P ↔ Q, one proves both P → Q and Q → P. Either statement can then replace the other within that setting, although one may be easier to understand or use.
equivalence.rule: A single implication gives a reduction in one direction, not an equivalence.
equivalence.deep: The papers use equivalences to compare reformulations of open problems. An equivalent reformulation preserves the unresolved question; proving the equivalence alone does not establish either side unconditionally.

erdos.label: Paul Erdős
erdos.preview: Paul Erdős was a mathematician known for work in number theory, combinatorics, probability, and related fields.
erdos.card: He posed and collected many problems, often through extensive collaboration. The site studies selected questions identified by their numbers in the independently maintained Erdős Problems database.
erdos.rule: A database number identifies the question; it does not describe its current solution status.
erdos.deep: Read the linked problem statement and references for the intended formulation. A paper may establish a related theorem, special case, or obstruction while the numbered question remains open.

erdos_problem.label: Erdős problem
erdos_problem.preview: An Erdős problem is a mathematical question associated with Paul Erdős; this site uses the numbering of the Erdős Problems database.
erdos_problem.card: For example, “Erdős #249” identifies a particular database entry rather than the 249th theorem in this repository. The entry supplies the question and references needed to understand its origin and context.
erdos_problem.rule: Compare a paper's exact statement with the original question before interpreting a result as a solution.
erdos_problem.deep: An equivalent reformulation, a finite computation, and an unconditional proof are different forms of progress and should retain their own descriptions.

euler_product.label: euler product
euler_product.preview: An Euler product expresses a quantity as a product of factors associated with individual primes.
euler_product.card: For example, the sum of 1/n² over positive integers equals the product of (1−1/p²)⁻¹ over primes p. Unique prime factorisation explains the correspondence: expanding the factors selects each integer exactly once.
euler_product.rule: Infinite products and rearrangements require convergence justifications; a finite product over the prime divisors of one integer has a different scope.
euler_product.deep: The totient formula φ(n) = n∏_{p∣n}(1−1/p) is a finite example. The papers use these separate prime contributions to analyse divisibility and the dependence of totient values on residue classes.

eulers_theorem_modular.label: Euler's theorem (modular arithmetic)
eulers_theorem_modular.preview: Euler's theorem says that if a is coprime to a positive integer n, then a raised to φ(n) is congruent to 1 modulo n.
eulers_theorem_modular.card: The totient φ(n) counts integers from 1 through n that are coprime to n. For example, φ(10) = 4 and 3⁴ = 81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 10.
eulers_theorem_modular.deep: The exponent φ(n) gives a period but need not be the smallest one. The papers use such exponents to arrange modular repetition while separately proving any claim about the exact multiplicative order.

evaluator.label: evaluator
evaluator.preview: An evaluator is a tool or procedure that assesses something against chosen criteria.
evaluator.card: In Plectis's component model, an evaluator observes inputs and reports its assessment without changing the material being assessed. A separate action is responsible for any repair or update.
evaluator.rule: The criteria determine what its result can establish.
evaluator.deep: For example, an evaluator may detect that a generated page disagrees with source data. Its report identifies the mismatch; it does not by itself decide that the page, source, or generation rule should be changed.

eventual_property.label: eventual property
eventual_property.preview: An eventual property holds at every index after some finite threshold.
eventual_property.card: For a sequence indexed by natural numbers, “eventually P(n)” means that there is an N such that P(n) holds for all n ≥ N. Any failures must occur before that threshold.
eventual_property.rule: This is stronger than holding infinitely often or at arbitrarily large indices.
eventual_property.deep: For example, being positive holds eventually for n − 10, whereas being even never holds eventually for all integers n. The papers use this distinction when comparing recurring obstructions with consequences of rationality.

evidence.label: evidence
evidence.preview: Evidence is information that supports or challenges a particular claim.
evidence.card: It may come from a source, observation, proof, calculation, or recorded test. Plectis links claims to their evidence so readers can examine the basis and decide whether it supports the wording used.
evidence.rule: Evidence should be interpreted within the conditions under which it was obtained.
evidence.deep: A test result, for instance, concerns the version, inputs, and environment tested. A proof has a different scope, determined by its precise statement and assumptions.

evidence_band.label: evidence band
evidence_band.preview: An evidence band labels the kind of support attached to a statement in a mathematical working record.
evidence_band.card: The records use labels such as Lean for formal checking, Cert for a checked certificate, Math for mathematical argument, Cited for a referenced result, and Open for an unresolved obligation.
evidence_band.rule: These labels describe different sources of support, not interchangeable levels of approval.
evidence_band.deep: A separate scope description indicates whether the statement covers listed cases, a bounded range, arbitrarily large parameters, or all allowed parameters. Both the evidence and its reach matter.

exact_rational_arithmetic.label: exact rational arithmetic
exact_rational_arithmetic.preview: Exact rational arithmetic calculates with integer numerators and denominators instead of rounded decimal values.
exact_rational_arithmetic.card: For example, 1/3 + 1/6 is stored and simplified to 1/2 using integer operations. Provided the implementation supports the required integer sizes, these operations introduce no rounding error.
exact_rational_arithmetic.rule: Exact calculation still depends on correct inputs, algorithms, and interpretation.
exact_rational_arithmetic.deep: The papers use it when a tiny difference or precise equality matters. It settles the computed rational expression, while an argument about an infinite limit may also need a proved bound on the omitted terms.

executable_cross_section.label: executable cross-section
executable_cross_section.preview: An executable cross-section is a selected part of a larger system that can be run and inspected on its own.
executable_cross_section.card: Plectis publishes components with the source, inputs, checks, and records needed to examine their behaviour. The selection aims to make a working mechanism available without requiring the entire private environment.
executable_cross_section.rule: Its scope is the included material and the dependencies declared for it.
executable_cross_section.deep: A successful run provides evidence about that public selection. Claims about the larger system need their own support, especially where unpublished components or interactions are involved.

execution.label: execution
execution.preview: Execution is the running of instructions or the actual performance of a planned operation.
execution.card: Source code, a command, or a workflow description records intended work; execution is the event in which a computer or actor carries it out with particular inputs and conditions.
execution.rule: A plan or runnable artifact does not establish that execution began, reached its final step, or produced the intended result.
execution.deep: Execution occurs in a concrete environment and can differ from the plan because of inputs, configuration, permissions, dependencies, timing, or failure. It may finish successfully, stop partway, remain active, or complete with unwanted side effects. Logs and receipts can show which instructions ran, while outputs and state checks show what changed. A successful process exit establishes only the success condition defined by that process; it does not automatically prove semantic correctness, publication, deployment, or acceptance by another system.

existential_quantifier.label: existential quantifier
existential_quantifier.preview: An existential quantifier states that at least one element of a specified domain satisfies a property.
existential_quantifier.card: The symbol ∃ means “there exists.” To establish ∃n ∈ ℕ, n² = 4, the number 2 is a witness. “At least one” does not mean exactly one: a separate uniqueness claim is needed to exclude other witnesses.
existential_quantifier.rule: A witness must satisfy every required condition; changing the domain can change whether a witness exists.
existential_quantifier.deep: In ∀x ∃y, the choice of y may depend on x. In ∃y ∀x, one y must work for all x. Lean statements preserve this distinction, which can make a conditional or uniform claim substantially stronger.

exit_code.label: exit code
exit_code.preview: An exit code is the small numeric status a process returns when it finishes.
exit_code.card: By convention zero usually reports success and nonzero values distinguish kinds of failure, though each program defines its own meanings. Scripts and workflow engines use the code to decide whether to continue, retry, or stop. Output text and exit status are separate evidence.
exit_code.rule: An exit code must be interpreted using the producing command’s contract; nonzero does not always mean the same failure, and zero does not validate claims beyond that command.
exit_code.deep: An exit code is a process-level completion signal, usually an integer made available to the parent shell or orchestrator. Unix convention reserves zero for success and nonzero values for exceptional outcomes, but individual programs define the detailed mapping. Standard output and error text may explain the result yet remain separate from this status. Signals, crashes, wrappers, pipelines, and timeouts can transform what callers observe. Reliable automation therefore interprets codes through the command’s documented contract and preserves enough output to diagnose which condition actually occurred.

exogenous.label: exogenous
exogenous.preview: Exogenous means originating outside the system or process under discussion.
exogenous.card: An external observation, event, or judgement can be exogenous relative to the process being studied. The classification depends on the chosen boundary: a signal can be external to one component but internal to the organisation containing it.
exogenous.rule: Outside origin does not by itself guarantee accuracy or independence.
exogenous.deep: Plectis uses the term when discussing evidence and criticism that do not arise solely from the workflow producing the work. The source's expertise and dependencies still need assessment.

exogenous_truth.label: exogenous truth
exogenous_truth.preview: “Exogenous truth” is this project's phrase for judgement brought in from outside the process being judged.
exogenous_truth.card: It refers to an independent reader examining the public evidence and forming their own assessment, including disagreement with the project's account. The phrase stresses an external source of criticism or correction.
exogenous_truth.rule: It does not mean that an outsider's judgement is automatically true.
exogenous_truth.deep: The value lies in different evidence, expertise, or assumptions entering the discussion. A claim still needs to be assessed on its merits, whether it comes from inside or outside the project.

exponent.label: exponent
exponent.preview: An exponent specifies a power: in bⁿ, b is the base and n is the exponent.
exponent.card: For a positive integer n, bⁿ means multiplying n copies of b. With nonzero b, b⁰ = 1 and b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. Fractional and real exponents require further definitions and domain conditions.
exponent.rule: In digit expansions and arithmetic series, check whether the exponent is restricted to integers.
exponent.deep: The expression 2ⁿ − 1 subtracts one after taking the power. It differs from 2ⁿ⁻¹, which lowers the exponent before calculating the power.

exponential_growth.label: exponential growth
exponential_growth.preview: Exact exponential growth multiplies a positive quantity by the same factor greater than one at each step.
exponential_growth.card: For example, 2ⁿ doubles with each unit increase of n and eventually exceeds every fixed power nᵏ. Papers also use exponential upper or lower bounds, such as aₙ ≤ C·2ⁿ; such a bound does not say aₙ itself doubles each step.
exponential_growth.rule: The base, input variable, and direction of the bound matter; exponential growth is not a synonym for any rapid growth.
exponential_growth.deep: Moduli and carry barriers in the Mersenne-support work operate on exponential scales, making polynomial savings insufficient.

exposition.label: exposition
exposition.preview: Mathematical exposition explains a result, its proof, and why the argument works for its intended readers.
exposition.card: Good exposition states the assumptions, introduces notation, identifies the main idea, and distinguishes new work from earlier results. It makes a proof easier to assess and use without weakening its precise claim.
exposition.rule: Clear writing supports verification but cannot replace missing mathematical reasoning.
exposition.deep: The site treats exposition as a separate task from obtaining a checked proof. A formal declaration may be valid while still needing an explanation that lets another mathematician understand or continue the work.

factor.label: factor
factor.preview: A factor is one of the quantities multiplied together to make a product.
factor.card: In 12 = 3·4, both 3 and 4 are factors of 12. For integers, saying that d is a factor of n usually means that d divides n exactly.
factor.rule: Factorisation expresses an object as a product of its factors.
factor.deep: In algebra, factors may be expressions: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1). The setting determines which factors count as irreducible and what uniqueness of factorisation means. Factoring can expose roots or divisibility conditions that are hidden in the expanded expression.

factorial.label: factorial
factorial.preview: The factorial of a nonnegative integer n is the product of the integers from 1 through n, with the value at zero defined as 1.
factorial.card: For example, 4! = 24. Factorials count arrangements of n distinct objects and also provide rapidly growing, highly divisible denominators in number-theory problems.
factorial.rule: The exclamation mark here is mathematical notation, not punctuation indicating emphasis.
factorial.deep: Expressions such as n! − 1 and (n − 1)! have very different values and divisibility properties. The paper's parentheses and order of operations are therefore part of the statement being studied.

factorisation.label: factorisation
factorisation.preview: Factorisation writes a number or algebraic expression as a product of simpler factors.
factorisation.card: For example, 60 = 2²·3·5 is the prime factorisation of 60. Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, apart from the order in which its factors are written.
factorisation.rule: Uniqueness depends on the mathematical setting when the objects are more general than integers.
factorisation.deep: The papers use factorisation to study divisibility, common factors, and the denominators of sums. A convenient factorisation can reveal constraints that are hard to see from a decimal value.

fail_closed.label: fail-closed
fail_closed.preview: Fail-closed means withholding an action when a required condition cannot be established.
fail_closed.card: For example, a publication gate may stop when a required check is missing or its result cannot be read. Plectis uses this behaviour where proceeding without evidence would wrongly treat uncertainty as permission.
fail_closed.rule: The required conditions and the action being withheld must be explicit.
fail_closed.deep: Failing closed can prevent an unsupported action, but it does not prove the underlying artifact is faulty. The next step may be to obtain the missing evidence or repair the check.

failure_class_propagation.label: failure class propagation
failure_class_propagation.preview: Failure-class propagation checks whether a discovered fault also affects other cases for the same reason.
failure_class_propagation.card: Plectis starts with the local failure, identifies its cause, and inspects related surfaces that share the relevant mechanism. Confirmed instances can then be repaired together through the common source or rule.
failure_class_propagation.rule: Similarity alone is not enough to assume that another case has the same fault.
failure_class_propagation.deep: The aim is to fix a recurring cause without expanding the repair to unrelated work. A useful record states which cases were examined and where the explanation stops applying.

failure_modes.label: failure modes
failure_modes.preview: Failure modes are the distinct ways something can fail to meet its intended purpose.
failure_modes.card: A check might accept bad input, reject good input, use stale data, or fail to run. These are different failure modes because their causes, evidence, and repairs can differ.
failure_modes.rule: Name the mechanism of failure, not just the fact that a result is wrong.
failure_modes.deep: Plectis uses negative cases and recorded incidents to make such failures inspectable. Covering known modes improves a check, while new situations may still reveal modes that were not anticipated.

fallback.label: fallback
fallback.preview: A fallback is an alternative behavior used when a preferred route is unavailable, unsuitable, or fails.
fallback.card: A service may use cached data when a live provider is down, or switch to a simpler algorithm when resources are limited. The result can remain useful while losing freshness, accuracy, capacity, or assurance.
fallback.rule: Fallback behavior is defined by its trigger, alternative source or method, preserved capabilities, reduced guarantees, duration, and route back to normal operation.
fallback.deep: Fallbacks improve resilience when their reduced contract is explicit. A silent fallback can instead hide primary failures, make stale results look current, or produce inconsistent behavior across users. The alternative may fail independently or depend on the same underlying resource, so it is not automatically redundant. Systems often record fallback activation, expose degraded status, bound how long cached or approximate results remain acceptable, and test recovery. A fallback is a planned contingency, whereas arbitrary error swallowing merely conceals failure.

falsifiable.label: falsifiable
falsifiable.preview: A claim is falsifiable when some possible evidence could count against it under stated assumptions.
falsifiable.card: Falsifiability makes disagreement operational: the claim states conditions under which evidence would count against it. It does not mean the claim is false, easily tested, or scientifically important, and a failed test may also expose faulty assumptions or measurement.
falsifiable.rule: Falsifiable does not mean false; it means the claim states what evidence would conflict with it rather than accommodating every possible outcome.
falsifiable.deep: A falsifiable claim exposes at least one possible observation, experiment, counterexample, or result that would count against it under stated assumptions. This does not mean the claim is false, likely false, easy to test, or scientifically valuable. A negative result may challenge an auxiliary assumption, measurement method, or experimental setup instead of the central proposition, so interpretation still requires care. Conversely, repeatedly accommodating every outcome without changing the claim removes empirical content. Good statements identify both the conflicting evidence and the background conditions needed for that conflict to be meaningful.

farey_sequence.label: Farey sequence
farey_sequence.preview: The Farey sequence of order N lists all reduced fractions between 0 and 1 whose positive denominators are at most N.
farey_sequence.card: The fractions appear in increasing order, including 0/1 and 1/1. For example, order 3 gives 0/1, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 1/1.
farey_sequence.rule: “Reduced” means that numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than 1.
farey_sequence.deep: The denominator bound makes the sequence finite. Its neighbouring fractions have useful arithmetic relationships, making Farey sequences a way to organise questions about rational approximation and the gaps between fractions.

feedback_loop.label: feedback loop
feedback_loop.preview: A feedback loop occurs when a process's output influences its later behaviour.
feedback_loop.card: Feedback can reinforce a change, counteract it, or create more complicated dynamics. In software, test results can guide revisions; in research, an interpretation can shape which evidence is sought next.
feedback_loop.rule: Feedback is not inherently beneficial or self-confirming; its effect depends on what is measured and how it is used.
