provider.rule: The provider role is defined by what is supplied, to whom, through which interface, and under which availability, authorization, or usage conditions.
provider.deep: Providers may supply compute, models, identity, data, payment processing, storage, or local library functions. The same system can consume one service and provide another. Availability of a provider does not guarantee a particular answer, response time, capacity, price, or continued contract. Those properties belong to separate service terms and observed behavior. When results depend on an external provider, the interface version, request conditions, returned evidence, and failure modes determine what can be reproduced or independently checked.

pull_request.label: pull request
pull_request.preview: A pull request proposes merging a set of repository changes and provides a place to review them.
pull_request.card: It identifies source and target branches, displays their difference, carries discussion and automated checks, and records a merge or closure decision. Its displayed diff can change as the source branch changes. A pull request is a review and integration object, not the underlying commits themselves.
pull_request.rule: Approval or green checks cover the reviewed state and declared policies; they do not guarantee correctness or mean the proposal has been merged or deployed.
pull_request.deep: A pull request is a repository-hosting review object proposing that one branch or set of commits be integrated into another. It presents a comparison, discussion, automated checks, review decisions, and eventual merge or closure status. Because contributors can update the source branch, the displayed diff and tested head may change during review; approvals may become stale under project policy. The request is not itself a commit, branch, release, or deployment. Reliable references identify the reviewed revision, target, and whether the proposed content was ultimately merged.

pytest.label: pytest
pytest.preview: pytest is a framework for writing and running automated tests in Python.
pytest.card: It discovers tests, provides fixtures and assertions, and reports which tests pass or fail. Projects can also use plugins to extend its behaviour.
pytest.rule: A passing run concerns the selected tests in the environment and source version used.
pytest.deep: Plectis links runnable checks and result records so readers can inspect what was tested. A test suite may miss behaviours outside its coverage, so its pass should support specific claims rather than be treated as proof of complete correctness.

queryable.label: queryable
queryable.preview: Information is queryable when a reader or program can retrieve relevant items by asking a structured question or searching.
queryable.card: Plectis uses identifiers, fields, indexes, and relationships so material can be found without already knowing its exact file path. A query may return a summary with a route to fuller evidence.
queryable.rule: The query's coverage and matching rules affect what its results mean.
queryable.deep: No result can mean “not present in this indexed collection” rather than “does not exist”. Source routes and clear coverage help a reader decide when a broader search is needed.

queue.label: queue
queue.preview: A queue is a collection of waiting items managed for later processing under stated ordering and delivery rules.
queue.card: A print queue holds jobs until a printer can handle them. Software queues may prioritize urgent work, delay scheduled items, distribute jobs among workers, or redeliver an item after failed acknowledgement.
queue.rule: Queue behavior depends on ordering, capacity, ownership, acknowledgement, delivery guarantees, retry policy, and how completed or abandoned items are removed.
queue.deep: A queue need not be first-in, first-out. Priority, fairness, deadlines, partitioning, dependencies, and worker availability may change which item runs next. Queues absorb bursts and coordinate concurrent workers, but they can also accumulate delay or hide stalled work. At-most-once delivery may lose an item; at-least-once delivery may duplicate processing; exactly-once effects usually require additional transactional or idempotent design. Queue length alone does not show throughput, age of work, blocking dependencies, or successful completion.

quickstart.label: quickstart
quickstart.preview: A quickstart gives the shortest supported sequence of steps to obtain a first useful result.
quickstart.card: For a repository, that usually means getting the source, installing the declared dependencies, running an example or check, and inspecting its output. It should state any prerequisites needed for those steps.
quickstart.rule: The example establishes an initial working route, not mastery of the whole project.
quickstart.deep: A good quickstart leads onward to the explanation and reference material needed for further work. Its commands should be tested from a clean environment so hidden local setup does not become the reader's problem.

radix.label: radix
radix.preview: Radix is another word for the base of a positional numeral system.
radix.card: Decimal has radix ten and binary has radix two. In radix b, successive places have weights that are powers of b; the radix point separates whole-number places from fractional places.
radix.rule: The familiar decimal point is the radix point in base ten.
radix.deep: For integer bases greater than one, rational numbers have eventually periodic expansions. The value is independent of its chosen radix, although its digits and period can change substantially when written in another base.

rank_of_matrix.label: rank of a matrix
rank_of_matrix.preview: The dimension of the space spanned by a matrix's rows or columns.
rank_of_matrix.card: A matrix with at least one nonzero column and every column proportional to it has rank one. The n×n identity matrix has rank n. Rank counts independent directions retained by the corresponding linear map.
rank_of_matrix.rule: Row rank equals column rank. A nonzero k×k minor proves rank at least k, while all minors of order k+1 vanishing proves rank at most k. The rank cannot exceed either matrix dimension.
rank_of_matrix.deep: Evaluation matrices turn arithmetic functions into finite linear-algebra objects. Proving large rank shows many channels are independent; it does not by itself establish irrationality of an infinite sum, which requires a separate analytic or denominator bridge.

rational.label: rational
rational.preview: A rational number is a number equal to a/b for integers a and nonzero b.
rational.card: Examples include 3/4, −2, and 0. Fractions differing by a common nonzero factor can represent the same rational number; a positive denominator and lowest terms provide a standard representation.
rational.rule: In any integer base greater than one, rational numbers have terminating or eventually repeating digit expansions.
rational.deep: An infinite series of rational terms can have a rational or irrational sum. The type of each term alone does not determine the type of the limit.

rational_approximation.label: rational approximation
rational_approximation.preview: Rational approximation studies how closely fractions can approach a number, especially in relation to their denominators.
rational_approximation.card: For example, 22/7 approximates π with a small error, but the denominator 7 matters when comparing its quality with other approximations. A useful estimate states both the error and how it depends on q in p/q.
rational_approximation.rule: A small decimal error alone does not establish irrationality.
rational_approximation.deep: Arguments in these papers combine structured approximations with denominator restrictions or tail bounds. The theorem must explain why their combined behaviour cannot occur if the target number is rational.

raw_seed.label: raw seed
raw_seed.preview: Raw seed is Plectis's preserved, append-only record of the operator's original words and developing ideas.
raw_seed.card: Later summaries, interpretations, and rules can refer back to it, while the original material remains available for checking intent and context. Corrections or changes of mind are preserved as further input rather than silently replacing the earlier record.
raw_seed.rule: Agent-authored synthesis belongs in a separate attributed record.
raw_seed.deep: Raw seed is authoritative about what the operator said. Claims about software behaviour, mathematics, or external facts still require the appropriate implementation or factual evidence rather than authority from a quotation alone.

reader.label: reader
reader.preview: A reader is the person or software consuming a document or other published material.
reader.card: The reader may be new to the subject, seeking one fact, reviewing a proof, or preparing to run a check. Different purposes call for different amounts of context and detail.
reader.rule: Plectis's summaries and source routes should make those different reading paths possible.
reader.deep: Defining specialist terms helps a non-specialist proceed without interrupting an expert. The surrounding explanation should still be understandable enough that a glossary is optional support rather than a prerequisite for every sentence.

reader_packet.label: reader packet
reader_packet.preview: A reader packet gathers selected explanations, links, source references, and scope information for someone examining the project.
reader_packet.card: It can be downloaded or supplied to an assistant as a portable starting point. The selection helps the reader orient and identify which original material deserves closer attention.
reader_packet.rule: The packet is a generated guide with declared coverage, not a replacement for all its sources.
reader_packet.deep: Its version matters when the project changes. A useful packet preserves routes to current source and evidence while identifying which summaries or copied contents belong to the packet's own snapshot.

readiness.label: readiness
readiness.preview: Readiness is the condition of meeting the stated requirements for a particular next action or operating stage.
readiness.card: A readiness decision compares current state with a declared gate for testing, review, publication, deployment, or operation. Evidence supports the decision, but the evidence itself is not readiness and one stage does not imply another.
readiness.rule: Readiness is relative to a named action and its required conditions; it holds when those conditions are satisfied, and it ends when a requirement fails or the target conditions change.
readiness.deep: Readiness describes whether an artifact, service, or process currently satisfies the conditions for a specified next step. A test-ready change may need required files and a working build; publication readiness may add source checks and review; production readiness may require operational capacity, rollback, security, and monitoring. Test reports, approvals, freshness records, and health signals are evidence used to judge those conditions, rather than readiness itself. Because gates differ, passing an earlier one cannot silently confer a stronger status. A readiness result also becomes stale when dependencies, requirements, or the evaluated artifact change.

real_number.label: real number
real_number.preview: A real number is a point on the real number line, including rational and irrational values.
real_number.card: Integers, fractions, √2, and π are examples. The real numbers provide a setting for limits, lengths, and continuous quantities; they are commonly denoted by ℝ.
real_number.rule: Real does not mean that a number has a finite decimal representation or can be computed exactly by a program.
real_number.deep: In a paper, a real-valued series can converge without its sum being rational. Establishing the existence of the sum and classifying that value are separate questions.

receipt.label: receipt
receipt.preview: A receipt is a saved record of an action and its reported outcome.
receipt.card: Plectis uses receipts to identify what ran or changed, the relevant inputs, and the checks performed. The record gives later readers something concrete to compare with a completion claim.
receipt.rule: The strength of the evidence depends on how the receipt was produced and what it captures.
receipt.deep: A receipt is not automatically proof that every reported fact is true. Source versions, execution traces, and independent checks can help establish whether it accurately describes the action.

reciprocal.label: reciprocal
reciprocal.preview: The reciprocal of a nonzero number x is 1/x.
reciprocal.card: Multiplying a number by its reciprocal gives 1. For example, the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4, and the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.
reciprocal.rule: Zero has no reciprocal in the real or rational numbers.
reciprocal.deep: The papers study sums of reciprocals of structured integer sequences. The denominator's growth and arithmetic properties both matter: shrinking terms alone do not prove that a reciprocal series converges or determine whether its sum is rational.

reciprocal_series.label: reciprocal series
reciprocal_series.preview: A reciprocal series is a sum whose terms have the form 1/aₙ for specified nonzero numbers aₙ.
reciprocal_series.card: For example, ∑ 1/2ⁿ starting at n = 1 sums to 1, while ∑ 1/n diverges. The way the denominators grow influences convergence, but a precise comparison or other argument is needed.
reciprocal_series.rule: Convergence does not determine whether the sum is rational or irrational.
reciprocal_series.deep: The papers study denominators built from factorials, primes, or powers minus one. Their divisibility structure can constrain cancellation and rationality even when convergence follows from a simple size estimate.

recurrence.label: recurrence
recurrence.preview: A recurrence defines terms of a sequence through a relation involving other terms, usually earlier ones.
recurrence.card: Initial values together with the rule determine the sequence when the recurrence is well-posed. For example, a₀ = 1 and aₙ₊₁ = 2aₙ produce 1, 2, 4, 8, … .
recurrence.rule: The initial conditions are part of the definition.
recurrence.deep: The same recurrence can produce different sequences from different starting values. A direct formula may be proved equivalent to the recurrence, making it easier to establish growth, divisibility, or periodicity.

reduction.label: reduction
reduction.preview: A reduction shows how solving one problem would allow another problem to be solved.
reduction.card: If the target is P and the proposed replacement is Q, proving Q → P gives a route from a solution of Q to a solution of P. It can reveal a useful sufficient condition.
reduction.rule: That direction alone does not show that P and Q are equivalent.
reduction.deep: The replacement may be harder, stronger, or even impossible under its own conditions. The papers should state the direction and any reverse implication before treating a reduction as the same unresolved problem.

reference.label: reference
reference.preview: A reference identifies another source, object, or location relevant to the current material.
reference.card: It can be a citation, link, stable identifier, file path, or declaration name. Plectis uses references to connect summaries with the material needed to inspect them.
reference.rule: A useful reference identifies both the destination and why it is relevant.
reference.deep: Its presence alone does not show that the destination supports the claim. Readers may need a particular section, theorem, version, or execution record to check the precise relationship being asserted.

reformulation.label: reformulation
reformulation.preview: A reformulation expresses a question or statement in a different way, ideally making a useful aspect of its structure clearer.
reformulation.card: When two formulations are claimed to be equivalent, a proof must show that each implies the other under the stated assumptions. A one-way relationship instead gives a sufficient or necessary condition.
reformulation.rule: Changing notation or coordinates does not by itself resolve an open question.
reformulation.deep: The papers use reformulations to expose exact obligations and compare attempted approaches. The relationship to the original target should remain visible so a reader can tell what proving the new statement would accomplish.

registry.label: registry
registry.preview: A registry is a structured collection of identified records about a particular kind of object.
registry.card: It provides stable names and fields that tools can query, validate, and use to build other views. Plectis has registries for objects such as terms, components, and claims.
registry.rule: A registry's schema and ownership rules determine what its entries mean.
registry.deep: Registration can establish that an item has been recorded without establishing that it is complete, approved, or correct. Those statuses require explicit fields and the appropriate evidence or decision process.

regression.label: regression
regression.preview: Regression means either lost software behaviour after a change or a statistical method that models an outcome from predictor variables.
regression.card: A software regression is behaviour that once worked and later broke; a regression test preserves a case that should continue working. Statistical regression estimates how an outcome varies with one or more predictors.
regression.rule: Software regression requires comparison across versions, whereas statistical regression requires a fitted response-and-predictor model; neither meaning by itself establishes the cause of an observed outcome.
regression.deep: In software, a regression occurs when a change damages behaviour that a previous version provided. A regression test records the expected behaviour so later runs can detect its return. In statistics, regression is a family of methods for estimating or predicting a response from explanatory variables, with assumptions that depend on the chosen model. A fitted association does not alone prove causation, and a low prediction error does not validate every model assumption. The two senses share a word but describe different objects, so terms such as version, test, coefficient, predictor, and residual determine the intended meaning.

regression_test.label: regression test
regression_test.preview: A regression test checks that previously expected software behaviour still works after a change.
regression_test.card: A test can preserve a fixed bug’s reproducing case or another established requirement. For example, a glossary test can check that a specific phrase still opens the right definition after the matching code changes.
regression_test.rule: A passing regression test covers its tested conditions; it does not show that all prior behaviour has been preserved.
regression_test.deep: A useful regression test exercises an observable requirement with inputs that would reveal the relevant breakage. The expected result must be justified independently of the current implementation, or the test can merely repeat the same mistake. Regression tests often run in continuous integration. They differ from statistical regression, which estimates relationships between variables, and from a software regression, which is the defect rather than the check.

release.label: release
release.preview: A software release is an identified version or artifact set that a publisher makes available for others to use.
release.card: A release may package source, binaries, documentation, migration notes, and checksums under a version or tag. It can be available for download without being installed or deployed anywhere.
release.rule: Release status concerns publication of a named version and remains distinct from its source commit, build, deployment, announcement, support period, and external acceptance.
release.deep: Releases can be tags, packages, container images, website bundles, mobile builds, or coordinated sets of artifacts. The publisher selects what belongs, records changes, and supplies retrieval and integrity information. A prerelease can be public while explicitly unstable. Replacing an asset under the same label weakens reproducibility unless content hashes preserve identity. Publishing a release does not show that users upgraded, production deployed it, reviewers approved it, or every environment can run it. Those are separate states with their own evidence.

reliability.label: reliability
reliability.preview: Reliability is the degree to which something performs its stated function consistently under specified conditions over time.
reliability.card: For systems, reliability can concern failure rates or the probability of failure-free operation during a stated period. For measurements and judgments, it concerns consistency across repeated observations or raters. The workload, environment, duration, and definition of failure determine what a reported measure means.
reliability.rule: A reliable process can consistently produce the wrong result if its specification or method is flawed, so reliability evidence must be read alongside correctness and validity evidence.
reliability.deep: Engineering reliability concerns performing the required function without failure under stated conditions. Availability instead measures whether a service is usable when needed and can include restoration after failures; repairable systems can have high availability despite frequent interruptions. Statistical reliability describes consistency among measurements, raters, or test items. Repeated outcomes need not be valid measurements of the intended target. Useful evaluation samples relevant variation, distinguishes independent from correlated failures, and records the observation period and failure conditions.

rename_migration_receipt.label: rename migration receipt
rename_migration_receipt.preview: A rename migration receipt records the plan, outcome, and checks for moving or renaming stored material.
rename_migration_receipt.card: It identifies the affected paths and the references that may need updating, together with any rollback or remaining obligations. Plectis uses it to keep a migration understandable across sessions.
rename_migration_receipt.rule: The receipt's status distinguishes a planned or blocked change from one that completed.
rename_migration_receipt.deep: A completed record should be backed by the relevant checks. Recording success alone does not guarantee that every reference was found, so the tested scope and any omissions should remain explicit.

replay.label: replay
replay.preview: A replay repeats a recorded scenario to examine whether it produces the expected behaviour.
replay.card: Plectis replays provide defined inputs, actions, and expected outcomes for a component or workflow. They can exercise interactions across several steps rather than only a single isolated function.
replay.rule: The scenario and environment determine what the replay covers.
replay.deep: A matching result supports repeatability of that case. A replay may deliberately model only part of a live process, so its success should not be described as verification of unrepresented inputs or wider system behaviour.

repository.label: repository
repository.preview: A repository stores a project's tracked files and, in Git, the history of their recorded revisions.
repository.card: It can exist locally or be hosted for sharing. A working checkout exposes files for a selected revision, possibly with local edits that have not been committed.
repository.rule: A repository need not be public, and a local clone may contain only part of its history or contents.
repository.deep: The public links here identify source collections that readers can inspect or obtain. Reproducing a result requires the appropriate revision and setup, not just a repository with the same name.

reproducible.label: reproducible
reproducible.preview: A result is reproducible when someone can use the stated materials and method to obtain the same relevant outcome.
reproducible.card: For software checks, this usually requires a source version, inputs, dependencies, commands, and an account of expected outputs. Exact byte equality may be appropriate for some artifacts; other results need a stated tolerance or comparison rule.
reproducible.rule: The reproduction claim should say which outcome is expected to agree.
reproducible.deep: Randomness, external services, and environment differences can affect runs. Making those dependencies explicit helps a reader distinguish an actual discrepancy from an allowed variation.

research_shift.label: research shift
research_shift.preview: A research shift is a bounded period of work on a specific, inspectable mathematical task.
research_shift.card: The project's relay workflow starts from an identified public revision, selects a question, and returns a result with the source and checks needed for review. A person may use a coding agent to carry out parts of that work.
research_shift.rule: The return should distinguish a proof, a failed route, an experiment, and an unresolved proposal.
research_shift.deep: Attribution and exact starting state make the contribution easier to assess and combine with other work. Completing the shift does not imply solving the whole problem.

residue_class.label: residue class
residue_class.preview: A residue class modulo m consists of all integers congruent to one another modulo m.
residue_class.card: For example, the class of 2 modulo 5 contains …, −8, −3, 2, 7, 12, … . Any of these integers can represent the class, while 2 is its usual least nonnegative representative.
residue_class.rule: The modulus is part of the class's identity.
residue_class.deep: The papers use classes to describe repeated arithmetic conditions across infinitely many integers. Proving a statement for a representative requires showing that the property is preserved for the other members of its class.

result_record.label: result record
result_record.preview: A result record stores what a particular check or run examined and what it reported.
result_record.card: It identifies the tested claim, relevant inputs or source version, outcome, and limits. Plectis keeps these records so an execution can be inspected after its temporary terminal output is gone.
result_record.rule: A record describes that run, not every later run of the same command.
result_record.deep: Its reliability depends on the recording process and links to evidence. If the source or inputs change, a new run may be needed before the earlier result can support a current claim.

retry.label: retry
retry.preview: A retry repeats an operation after failure, uncertainty, or the absence of a usable response.
retry.card: Retrying can recover from a temporary network interruption or busy service, but a lost response may hide that the first attempt already succeeded, so repeating it can duplicate a charge, message, or write.
retry.rule: Retry behavior is determined by triggering outcomes, attempt limits, delay and backoff, idempotency, cancellation, and treatment of late or ambiguous results.
retry.deep: Retries are safe only when repeated attempts have acceptable effects. Read-only requests are often repeatable, while payments, messages, file creation, and increments can duplicate consequences unless they use an idempotency key or transaction. Exponential backoff and jitter reduce synchronized load, but they do not make permanent errors recoverable. A client timeout creates uncertainty rather than proof of failure. Correct retry handling records attempt identity, distinguishes transient from terminal errors, caps total effort, and reconciles results that arrive after another attempt begins.

reviewer_brief.label: reviewer brief
reviewer_brief.preview: The reviewer brief is a compact generated packet for someone assessing the public work.
reviewer_brief.card: It gathers the main orientation, claims, source routes, and stated limits so a reader or assistant can identify what deserves closer inspection. It is a starting point for review rather than a substitute for the papers and code.
reviewer_brief.rule: The brief's version determines which public state it describes.
reviewer_brief.deep: A useful brief separates evidence classes and open questions. That lets a reviewer choose an appropriate check instead of treating every item in the packet as equally established.

riemann_map.label: riemann map
riemann_map.preview: A bijective holomorphic map between a simply connected proper planar domain and the unit disc.
riemann_map.card: A Riemann map replaces a complicated simply connected planar region by the unit disc through a bijective holomorphic function. It preserves angles locally, so analytic estimates can be transported between the two coordinate pictures.
riemann_map.rule: The Riemann mapping theorem applies to a nonempty simply connected open region that is not the whole complex plane. A unique map requires normalization, commonly fixing one interior point and a derivative direction.
riemann_map.deep: The lemniscate paper maps a Jordan sublevel component to the disc, where inverse branches, energy integrals, and hyperbolic estimates are more explicit. The map preserves conformal structure, not ordinary Euclidean lengths or areas without scale factors.

rigidity.label: rigidity
rigidity.preview: A rigidity result shows that stated conditions leave an object unusually little freedom, often determining it up to a specified equivalence.
rigidity.card: The conclusion may force one exact form, a small family, or a structure preserved under allowed transformations. The hypotheses explain which apparent alternatives have been excluded.
rigidity.rule: Rigidity does not always mean literal uniqueness of one object.
rigidity.deep: For example, a geometric result may determine a shape only up to rotation or scaling. Reading that qualification is essential before interpreting a classification as saying that there is exactly one possible instance.

root_multiplicity.label: root multiplicity
root_multiplicity.preview: The multiplicity of a root measures how many copies of its linear factor occur in a polynomial.
root_multiplicity.card: For a nonzero polynomial, a root a has multiplicity k when p(z) = (z − a)ᵏq(z) with q(a) ≠ 0. A simple root has multiplicity one; a multiple root has larger multiplicity.
root_multiplicity.rule: Counting with multiplicity differs from counting distinct locations.
root_multiplicity.deep: For example, (z − 1)²(z + 2) has three roots counted with multiplicity but only two distinct roots. The distinction matters when a geometric argument chooses paths between root points. Repeated occurrences share one location and cannot be separated geometrically just by assigning them different labels.

polynomial_root.label: root of a polynomial
polynomial_root.preview: A number r for which a polynomial f has value f(r)=0.
polynomial_root.card: For f(z)=z²-1, both 1 and -1 are roots because substituting either gives zero. The factorization f(z)=(z-1)(z+1) displays them directly.
polynomial_root.rule: A nonconstant complex polynomial of degree n has n roots when repetitions are counted. A root can have multiplicity greater than one, as 0 does for z².
polynomial_root.deep: Problem 1041 asks whether two root occurrences can be joined by a short path staying in a prescribed polynomial sublevel set.

routing.label: routing
routing.preview: Routing chooses the next relevant destination or action from a question, input, or current state.
routing.card: In Plectis, a route may lead to a source file, a navigation collection, a governing skill, or the workflow responsible for a change. Its purpose is to reduce guesswork before deeper inspection.
routing.rule: The route must match the task's actual subject and authority requirements.
routing.deep: A plausible keyword match can still lead to the wrong owner. A useful route therefore supplies enough identity and explanation for the reader to recognise and correct a mismatch.

row_job.label: row job
row_job.preview: A row job specifies one bounded operation on an identified record or small artifact selection.
row_job.card: It states the target, intended change, permitted scope, expected result, and required check before execution. Plectis uses this structure to turn a broad request into work that can be assigned and assessed.
row_job.rule: The job description is a plan; a separate result records what actually happened.
row_job.deep: Fixing the scope in advance makes it easier to detect unintended changes or unmet requirements. The worker still needs to inspect the target and stop if the assumed conditions do not hold.

rowability.label: rowability
rowability.preview: Rowability is Plectis's term for whether a collection can be reliably browsed as identifiable, source-linked entries.
rowability.card: Each item needs a stable identity, useful summary, route to detail, and appropriate status information. Merely having files somewhere in the repository does not supply that browsing interface.
rowability.rule: The collection should acknowledge missing or unsupported views.
rowability.deep: This property matters when an agent must choose among many artifacts without guessing their names. A rowable collection turns discovery into selecting known options while retaining access to the source needed for the chosen task.

run.label: run
run.preview: A run is one execution of a command, program, test, or experiment.
run.card: It has particular inputs, a source version, an environment, and an outcome. Plectis records those details when they are needed to support a claim or repeat the work.
run.rule: Two runs of the same command need not be identical if their conditions differ.
run.deep: A run starting successfully is also different from completing successfully. The final status and relevant outputs determine what happened, while a readable record lets later work assess it without relying on a session summary.

runnable.label: runnable
runnable.preview: Runnable means the material can be executed with the stated code, dependencies, inputs, and instructions.
runnable.card: For a public component, the reader should be able to obtain the required files and perform the advertised command in a supported environment. Missing private setup would limit that claim.
runnable.rule: Being runnable does not mean that the run succeeds or establishes the intended property.
runnable.deep: Execution results and checks provide the next layer of evidence. The published instructions should say where the output appears and what outcome counts as success for the example.

running_lcm.label: running least common multiple
running_lcm.preview: A running least common multiple takes the least common multiple of all terms up to the current position in a positive-integer sequence.
running_lcm.card: For 2, 3, 4, the running values are 2, 6, 12. Each new value is the least common multiple of the previous running value and the next term.
running_lcm.rule: It changes only when the next term supplies a prime factor at a higher exponent than was previously required.
running_lcm.deep: The Erdős #269 work studies reciprocal sums involving these cumulative values. Their behaviour depends on the specified input sequence, not merely on how many terms have been included.

runtime.label: runtime
runtime.preview: A runtime is the software support and execution context used while a program runs.
runtime.card: The word can refer to language machinery, loaded code, active processes, or the current state of a workflow. Plectis distinguishes this live behaviour from static source files and documentation about intended behaviour.
runtime.rule: The relevant environment and version determine which runtime is being described.
runtime.deep: Inspecting source can explain what a program is meant to do, while runtime records show what a particular execution did. Both may be needed to understand an error or validate a fix.

saddle_connection.label: saddle connection
saddle_connection.preview: A saddle connection is a trajectory connecting saddle-type singular points, possibly returning to the same one.
saddle_connection.card: The trajectory is regular away from its endpoints, while the endpoints are understood through limiting behaviour or a separately defined extension. Such a connection depends on the global flow, not just the local shape of each saddle.
saddle_connection.rule: The vector field need not be defined at the endpoints under the same formula used between them.
saddle_connection.deep: For Newton flow, polynomial values along a regular trajectory differ by positive real scale factors. This constrains which nonzero critical values can occur at its limiting endpoints.

saddle_point.label: saddle point
saddle_point.preview: A critical point where a function rises in some directions and falls in others.
saddle_point.card: For u(x,y)=x²-y², the origin is a saddle point: u increases along the x-axis and decreases along the y-axis. It is critical because the gradient vanishes, but it is neither a local maximum nor minimum.
saddle_point.rule: A nondegenerate planar saddle has one rising and one falling direction in suitable local coordinates. Degenerate or multiple critical points may have more complicated prongs, so conclusions proved for simple saddles do not automatically extend.
saddle_point.deep: Polynomial sublevel components can merge at saddle levels. The associated separatrices and local branches describe how root-containing regions attach, while global path construction still requires controlling what happens outside the local saddle neighbourhood.

sandbox.label: sandbox
sandbox.preview: A sandbox is an environment that enforces specific limits on the files, networks, devices, processes, or privileges available to running code.
sandbox.card: Sandboxing reduces the reach of mistakes or hostile behaviour by restricting selected capabilities. Its protection is only as broad as the configured boundaries and the enforcement layer that maintains them.
sandbox.rule: A sandbox confines effects only across its enforced boundaries; allowed paths, network access, inherited credentials, host interfaces, and escape mechanisms remain inside its effective capability set.
sandbox.deep: A sandbox runs code with a constrained view of its surroundings. Depending on the design, it may limit filesystem paths, network destinations, system calls, devices, process creation, memory, time, or credentials. These restrictions reduce potential impact, but they do not establish that the code is correct or safe. A sandbox that permits writes to a shared directory still allows damage there, and a network-enabled sandbox can affect reachable services. Isolation also depends on correct configuration and enforcement; a vulnerability in the boundary can permit escape. Sandbox claims therefore describe concrete restrictions rather than absolute protection.

scalar.label: scalar
scalar.preview: A scalar is an element of the number system used for coefficients, scaling, and arithmetic in a mathematical structure.
scalar.card: Multiplying the vector (2,3) by the scalar 4 gives (8,12). Depending on the vector space, allowed scalars may be rational, real, or complex numbers.
scalar.rule: Scalar multiplication must obey distributive and associative laws with vector addition.
scalar.deep: The field of allowed scalars matters for linear independence: a family independent over the rationals may be dependent over the reals. In computing, “scalar” can instead distinguish a single value from a vector or array.

schema.label: schema
schema.preview: A schema defines the expected structure and constraints of data.
schema.card: It can specify required fields, permitted types, allowed values, and relationships between fields. Plectis uses schemas so tools can validate structured records and interpret them consistently.
schema.rule: Valid structure does not ensure that the recorded facts are true.
schema.deep: For example, a result record can contain all required fields while reporting the wrong outcome. Schema validation should therefore be paired with checks appropriate to the contents and the claim for which the record is used.

scope.label: scope
scope.preview: Scope states the cases, objects, actions, and conditions to which something applies.
scope.card: For a theorem, scope comes from its quantified variables and hypotheses. For a test, it includes the inputs and behaviour examined. For a task, it includes the authorised changes and intended result.
scope.rule: Evidence and permission should not silently extend beyond their stated scope.
scope.deep: Plectis records these boundaries so partial work can be useful without appearing universal. A clear scope also makes it easier to identify which additional evidence or authorisation would support a broader action.

semantic_naming.label: semantic naming
semantic_naming.preview: Semantic naming gives an identifier or label enough meaning to help a reader recognise the object's role.
semantic_naming.card: Plectis distinguishes stable identity, storage path, display label, and aliases so those functions can be maintained separately. A useful name can indicate a component's job without forcing the reader to open it first.
semantic_naming.rule: A name suggests meaning; the source record establishes the full role, authority, and current status.
semantic_naming.deep: Encoding changeable status into a permanent name can make it misleading. Explicit fields and detail routes are often better places for information that needs to change over time.

separatrix.label: separatrix
separatrix.preview: A separatrix is a distinguished trajectory, or invariant boundary, separating regions with different dynamical behaviour.
separatrix.card: Near a planar saddle, special incoming and outgoing trajectories divide families of nearby trajectories. They help describe which starting points can approach which limiting objects.
separatrix.rule: The precise definition depends on the dynamical system and the role of its singular points.
separatrix.deep: In the Newton-flow material, these paths are used to organise regions around roots and critical points. Their local directions do not alone prove the existence or shape of a global connection between two distant endpoints.

sequence.label: sequence
sequence.preview: A sequence is an indexed family of terms, usually ordered by natural-number positions.
sequence.card: For example, aₙ = 1/n for n ≥ 1 gives 1, 1/2, 1/3, … . The index identifies each position, and repeated values are allowed.
sequence.rule: The starting index and formula or recurrence are part of the definition.
sequence.deep: A sequence lists terms; a series adds them. That distinction matters because a sequence tending to zero can still have a divergent sum, as happens with the harmonic sequence and harmonic series.

series.label: series
series.preview: A mathematical series is a sum of terms from a sequence, often extending over infinitely many indices.
series.card: The expression ∑ aₙ is understood through its finite partial sums. When those partial sums approach a finite limit, the series converges and that limit is its sum.
series.rule: A time series is a different use: a sequence of observations indexed by time, not necessarily added together.
series.deep: The papers specify their summation indices and convergence conditions. Omitting the initial index or changing the order can matter, especially when terms are undefined or convergence is not absolute.

series_tail.label: series tail
series_tail.preview: The tail of a series is the part remaining after a chosen finite number of terms.
series_tail.card: For ∑ aₙ starting at 1, the tail after N is ∑ over n > N of aₙ. When the series converges, this equals the full sum minus its Nth partial sum.
series_tail.rule: A convergent series has tails tending to zero, although multiplying them by a growing factor may change that behaviour.
series_tail.deep: The papers often study scaled tails to expose integer or divisibility conditions. Those arithmetic properties require more than the fact that the unscaled tail becomes small.

set.label: set
set.preview: A set is a collection determined by which elements belong to it.
set.card: Order and repetition do not change a set: {1, 2} and {2, 1, 1} describe the same set. The notation x ∈ A says that x belongs to A.
set.rule: A sequence or multiset keeps information that an ordinary set discards.
set.deep: This distinction matters in the papers when selecting exponents or counting roots. A polynomial's roots as a set ignore repeated occurrences, while roots counted with multiplicity carry additional information.

set_intersection.label: set intersection
set_intersection.preview: The intersection of sets contains exactly the elements common to all of them.
set_intersection.card: For A = {1,2} and B = {2,3}, A ∩ B is {2}. If the sets have no common element, their intersection is empty. Membership in an intersection is an “and” condition: every participating membership requirement must hold.
set_intersection.rule: Two nonempty sets can have an empty intersection, so separate existence statements do not establish a common witness.
set_intersection.deep: The papers use intersections to combine restrictions on candidates, indices, or regions. Producing something that satisfies each condition separately can be much easier than producing one object satisfying all conditions together.

set_membership.label: set membership
set_membership.preview: Set membership is the relation saying that an object is one of the elements of a set.
set_membership.card: The symbol x ∈ A means “x belongs to A”; x ∉ A means it does not. For example, 2 ∈ {1,2,3}, but 5 ∉ {1,2,3}. Membership differs from subset inclusion: an element belongs to a set, whereas a subset contains only elements of that set.
set_membership.rule: An element can itself be a set, so braces and the declared types matter when reading nested collections.
set_membership.deep: Statements such as z ∈ U and n ∈ A specify which points or indices are allowed. These restrictions often carry the hypotheses needed for a formula, proof step, or chosen witness to be valid.

set_union.label: set union
set_union.preview: The union of sets contains every element belonging to at least one of them.
set_union.card: For A = {1,2} and B = {2,3}, the union A ∪ B is {1,2,3}. The shared element 2 appears once because sets record membership, not repeated occurrences. A union can also combine an infinite family of sets.
set_union.rule: Membership in a union is an “or” condition, allowing membership in several of the component sets.
set_union.deep: This differs from intersection, which requires simultaneous membership. In the mathematics pages, unions describe combined regions or collections of allowable cases; proving a property of each piece may require further work before it holds for the union.

shared_path.label: shared path
shared_path.preview: The shared path is the common way Plectis presents a component's claim, check, recorded result, and limits.
shared_path.card: Different components have different jobs, but readers can examine them through the same sequence: understand the assertion, inspect the test and inputs, read the output, and identify its scope.
shared_path.rule: The common presentation makes comparisons easier without making the components interchangeable.
shared_path.deep: Each component still needs evidence appropriate to its own mechanism. A shared card layout cannot substitute for a missing check or make one component inherit another's verified behaviour.

simple_critical_point.label: simple critical point
simple_critical_point.preview: A simple critical point of a complex polynomial p is a simple root of its derivative: p′(c) = 0 and p″(c) ≠ 0.
simple_critical_point.card: Near such a point, the first nonconstant term in the polynomial's local expansion is quadratic. This gives a specific local branching structure that differs from a higher-multiplicity critical point.
simple_critical_point.rule: When p(c) is nonzero, the associated modulus geometry has the ordinary nondegenerate saddle form.
simple_critical_point.deep: If p(c) = 0, the modulus instead vanishes there, so it should not be described by that same saddle claim. The papers' extra hypotheses distinguish these cases.

simply_connected.label: simply connected
simply_connected.preview: Path connected with every closed loop continuously shrinkable to a point inside the space.
simply_connected.card: A filled disc is simply connected. An annulus is not, because a loop encircling its hole cannot shrink without leaving the annulus.
simply_connected.rule: Connectedness alone does not rule out holes; simple connectivity adds precisely this global loop condition.
simply_connected.deep: Simply connected polynomial components admit Riemann maps and make holomorphic covering branches easier to continue globally.

simulation.label: simulation
simulation.preview: A simulation executes a model of a process to study the behaviour that follows from the model's rules and inputs.
simulation.card: Simulation permits controlled experiments when direct observation is costly, slow, dangerous, or impossible. Its results describe the modelled system and inherit the model's assumptions, simplifications, and parameter choices.
simulation.rule: A simulation result is conditional on the model, initial conditions, parameters, numerical method, and random inputs; agreement within the simulation is distinct from validation against observations of the target system.
simulation.deep: A simulation represents selected features of a process and calculates how that representation evolves. Deterministic simulations replay fixed equations or rules, while stochastic simulations sample uncertain events, often many times, to estimate a distribution of outcomes. Resolution, discretization, parameter choice, and random seeds can materially change the result. Verification asks whether the program implements the intended model; validation asks whether that model adequately represents the real system for the proposed use. A simulation can expose consequences, sensitivities, and failure modes without establishing that the same behaviour occurs outside the model.

skill.label: skill
skill.preview: In this system, a skill is a reusable set of instructions for carrying out a recognisable kind of task.
skill.card: It states when it applies, the steps to follow, relevant constraints, and routes to governing material. Agents can discover and reuse it instead of reconstructing the workflow from scratch.
skill.rule: A skill is procedural guidance; a component is implemented machinery that may carry out part of it.
skill.deep: The skill should stay aligned with the tools and rules it names. An instruction pointing to an obsolete command needs repair even if its general advice remains sound.

slice.label: slice
slice.preview: A slice is a selected part of a larger collection or system.
slice.card: Plectis uses the word for bounded sets of files, records, or components included in a task or public release. Naming the selection makes it clear what can be inspected or changed.
slice.rule: The selection's boundary should be explicit rather than inferred from its title.
slice.deep: A public slice can be independently runnable while the wider system remains unpublished. Evidence about that slice applies to its included material and tested interactions, with any broader conclusions requiring additional support.

smoke_check.label: smoke check
smoke_check.preview: A smoke check is a quick test for major failures in basic operation.
smoke_check.card: It might confirm that an application starts, an example command runs, or a key page loads. The aim is to catch obvious breakage before investing in more detailed checks.
smoke_check.rule: A smoke check deliberately has limited coverage.
smoke_check.deep: Its success is a useful first signal, not a comprehensive assessment of correctness. Plectis should identify the basic behaviour exercised so readers can tell which further checks are needed for a particular change.

smooth_function.label: smooth function
smooth_function.preview: A smooth function has continuous derivatives of every finite order in its stated mathematical setting.
smooth_function.card: Every polynomial is smooth, including at points where its first derivative is zero. Smoothness allows repeated differentiation but does not imply that a real function equals its Taylor series. A function can therefore be smooth without being analytic.
smooth_function.rule: Read smooth as C-infinity unless the source explicitly gives a finite differentiability class such as C-one or C-two.
smooth_function.deep: A smooth, or C-infinity, function has derivatives of every order and all those derivatives are continuous. For maps between Euclidean spaces, this means every iterated partial derivative exists and is continuous. On manifolds the definition is made through smooth coordinate charts. Smoothness is a regularity condition, not a claim of analyticity, convexity, or absence of critical points. In optimization prose, a smooth cell often means a region where the active formula and its derivatives vary smoothly; boundaries where the active branch changes may fail to share that regularity.

smooth_number.label: smooth number
smooth_number.preview: A positive integer is y-smooth if none of its prime factors exceeds y.
smooth_number.card: More generally, it is smooth over a specified set of primes if all its prime factors belong to that set. For example, 72 = 2³·3² is 3-smooth, while 70 has prime factors 2, 5, and 7.
smooth_number.rule: The bound or allowed prime set is part of the definition.
smooth_number.deep: The number 1 qualifies because it has no prime factors. The papers use smoothness to restrict which integers enter a sequence or reciprocal sum, often producing a structured but sparse collection.

snapshot.label: snapshot
snapshot.preview: A snapshot is a captured representation of data or system state associated with a particular point or version.
snapshot.card: A database snapshot can preserve records as they appeared at noon; a repository snapshot can preserve one commit. Later changes do not make that snapshot inaccurate, but they do make it stale as a description of current state.
snapshot.rule: Snapshot meaning depends on capture time, scope, consistency guarantees, source version, included external state, and whether content is copied or referenced immutably.
snapshot.deep: Snapshots support comparison, recovery, audit, and reproducibility by fixing a view that would otherwise change. They may be full copies, incremental differences, filesystem references, database-consistent views, or application exports. Capturing related systems at different moments can create an internally inconsistent composite. A snapshot also may omit caches, secrets, running processes, external services, or uncommitted changes. Restoring it recreates only the state actually captured, and a successful restore does not establish that newer dependent systems remain compatible.

software.label: software
software.preview: Software consists of programs and related data used by computers to perform tasks.
software.card: On this site, the software section presents Plectis's reusable research components and the machinery supporting its workflow. It is distinguished from the mathematical reading routes, although formal proofs also use software tools.
software.rule: Each published component needs its own description, dependencies, and evidence.
software.deep: A repository can make implementation available without demonstrating every advertised use. The source, runnable example, and recorded check together help a reader assess the particular behaviour being claimed.

library.label: software library
library.preview: A software library is a reusable collection of code, interfaces, or formal definitions intended for other programs or developments to use.
library.card: Libraries can be source packages, compiled objects, runtime modules, or formal collections such as Mathlib. Their exposed interfaces supply reusable operations or results. Consumers depend on the relevant version, behaviour, licence, and compatibility with other parts of their program or proof development.
library.rule: When a result depends on a software library, record the exact package, version or revision, relevant interface assumptions, and environment used.
library.deep: A library differs from an application because it primarily supplies capabilities to consumers rather than owning the whole interaction, although packages can contain both. Public interfaces form the supported contract; internal implementation may change between compatible releases. Static and dynamic libraries link differently, while interpreted packages load through a runtime. Formal libraries contribute checked definitions and theorems. Dependency updates can alter behavior or proof meaning, so reproducibility requires pinned identity and transitive dependencies, not merely the library’s familiar name.

source.label: source
source.preview: A source is the original or controlling material from which a particular claim or artifact is drawn.
source.card: Here it often means code, a structured record, a theorem declaration, or a document linked from a generated page. Which source matters depends on the question being asked.
source.rule: Source for implementation and source for human intent need not be the same material.
source.deep: A reliable explanation identifies the relevant source precisely, including a version where necessary. Opening it lets a reader check the detail that a summary may simplify or omit.

source_body.label: source body
source_body.preview: A source body is the actual content of the code or document being referenced.
source_body.card: In a component bundle, it can be the full function or module implementation, as distinct from its signature, description, path, or digest. Including the body makes direct inspection possible.
source_body.rule: The body needs an identifiable version and context to explain which material it represents.
source_body.deep: A function may also depend on imports, configuration, or other files outside its displayed body. The bundle should make those dependencies clear if readers are expected to reproduce its behaviour.

source_file.label: source file
source_file.preview: A source file contains material from which another artifact is built or defined.
source_file.card: Source files can be written by people or generated by tools. Their role as source is relative to the build or transformation being discussed.
source_file.rule: Being a source file does not automatically make it the editable authority for every workflow.
source_file.deep: Plectis identifies the owning source and builder so generated material can be refreshed correctly. Editing a generated source copy may be overwritten by the next update unless its upstream owner is changed.

source_slice.label: source slice
source_slice.preview: A source slice is the explicitly selected source material included in a task, package, or public release.
source_slice.card: It can contain files and dependencies needed to support particular pages, components, or results. Plectis publishes bounded slices so readers can inspect relevant machinery without receiving the entire private working repository.
source_slice.rule: The inventory determines what the slice includes and excludes.
source_slice.deep: Its claims should fit that selection. If an example relies on omitted material, the dependency must be disclosed or included before the example can be described as independently reproducible.

span.label: linear span
span.preview: In linear algebra, the span of a set of vectors is the set of all finite linear combinations of them.
span.card: A linear combination scales vectors by allowed scalars and adds the results. For example, two nonparallel vectors in the ordinary plane span the plane; one nonzero vector spans a line through the origin.
span.rule: A spanning family may contain redundant vectors and need not be a basis.
span.deep: The underlying field and vector space matter. Claims about dimension concern the amount of independent structure in the span, not merely how many vectors were listed.

sparse_checkout.label: sparse checkout
sparse_checkout.preview: A sparse checkout limits which tracked files Git places in the working directory.
sparse_checkout.card: It lets someone work on selected directories while the repository's history and object database may still cover a larger project. This can make a large checkout easier to navigate and use.
sparse_checkout.rule: Sparse checkout alone does not mean that only those files were downloaded.
sparse_checkout.deep: Reducing downloads is a separate capability of partial or filtered clones. The public instructions should distinguish those operations so readers understand which files are present locally and which data may still need to be fetched.

specification.label: specification
specification.preview: A specification states the requirements an implementation or result is expected to satisfy.
specification.card: It can define behaviour, data structure, interfaces, inputs, outputs, or permitted assumptions. A test or formal verification then checks some relationship between the implementation and those requirements.
specification.rule: The specification must itself express the intended task accurately.
specification.deep: A perfectly checked implementation of the wrong requirement can still fail the user's goal. Plectis therefore links requirements, source, and evidence so reviewers can examine both the check and the meaning of what it checks.

squarefree.label: squarefree
squarefree.preview: Squarefree means having no repeated prime factor for an integer, or no repeated irreducible factor for a nonzero polynomial.
squarefree.card: The integer 30=2·3·5 is squarefree, while 12=2²·3 is not. Over the complex numbers, a nonzero polynomial is squarefree exactly when every root is simple: (z−1)(z+1) qualifies, while (z−1)² does not.
squarefree.rule: The integer 1 and nonzero constant polynomials are squarefree; zero is not. Polynomial factors are taken over the specified coefficient field.
squarefree.deep: The same idea removes repeated factors in two settings. An irreducible polynomial factor cannot be split into lower-degree factors over its coefficient field. Over the complex numbers every nonconstant polynomial splits into linear factors, so squarefreeness becomes distinctness of roots, equivalently no common root of p and p′. The number-theory papers use squarefree integers in counting arguments, while the lemniscate papers use squarefree polynomials to control root geometry. These applications share a factorisation property without treating integers and polynomials as the same objects.

standard.label: standard
standard.preview: A standard specifies requirements that items or processes are expected to meet.
standard.card: Plectis stores standards as structured contracts covering fields, meanings, authority, validation, and maintenance. They give people and tools a common basis for writing and checking particular artifact kinds.
standard.rule: A standard states the requirement; evidence shows whether an item satisfies it.
standard.deep: The applicable version matters when rules change. A record valid under an earlier contract may need migration or a documented compatibility rule before it can be treated as valid under the current one.

statement_node.label: statement node
statement_node.preview: A statement node is one identified mathematical statement in a graph of results and their relationships.
statement_node.card: The graph can connect it to formal declarations, evidence, implications, and open obligations. Several declarations may support the same mathematical statement when they express equivalent versions or serve different implementation roles.
statement_node.rule: Grouping statements requires a justified correspondence, not just similar wording.
statement_node.deep: Plectis uses this distinction to make a large proof corpus easier to interpret. The number of declaration names need not equal the number of distinct claims or research ideas represented in the graph.

stationary_bootstrap.label: stationary bootstrap
stationary_bootstrap.preview: The stationary bootstrap resamples a time series in blocks of randomly chosen lengths to retain some of its temporal dependence.
stationary_bootstrap.card: In the standard construction, block lengths have a geometric distribution and starting points are sampled from the observed series, with circular continuation at its end. Joining such blocks creates a resampled series.
stationary_bootstrap.rule: Block length choices and assumptions about dependence affect the method's validity.
stationary_bootstrap.deep: It preserves local stretches of observations rather than exactly preserving every dependence in the original data. Statistical conclusions still require the sampling assumptions appropriate to the analysis.

stochastic.label: stochastic
stochastic.preview: Stochastic describes a process or model whose outcomes involve probability or randomness.
stochastic.card: A stochastic procedure can follow precise rules while producing different outcomes across runs because it samples random choices. Analysis describes distributions, expectations, variability, or event probabilities rather than one guaranteed path. Pseudorandom software also depends on a generator and seed.
stochastic.rule: Separate randomness in the model from uncertainty about the model, and record seeds when exact computational repetition matters.
stochastic.deep: A stochastic process, model, or algorithm includes outcomes governed by probability. Its rules may be exact even though individual runs differ, so analysis concerns distributions, expected values, variability, dependence, or event probabilities rather than one fixed path. Computational randomness is normally pseudorandom and becomes repeatable when the generator, seed, implementation, and relevant ordering are fixed. Stochastic variation differs from ignorance about model choice or data quality. A reported sample illustrates possible behavior; it does not alone characterize the underlying probability law or justify a causal conclusion.

stub.label: stub
stub.preview: A stub is a placeholder representing an item or interface whose full contents or behaviour are not yet supplied.
stub.card: It may allow navigation, compilation, or planning to proceed while showing where further work belongs. In testing, a stub can provide a simplified replacement for a dependency.
stub.rule: The placeholder's limitations should be explicit wherever its output is used.
stub.deep: A stub appearing in a catalog does not establish that the intended mechanism exists. Replacing it with an implementation requires the same source, interface, and validation checks as other substantive work.

subcover.label: subcover
subcover.preview: A subcover is a selection from a collection of covering sets that still covers the same target set.
subcover.card: If three open intervals cover [0,1] and two of those intervals already cover every point of [0,1], those two form a subcover. A finite subcover uses finitely many members of the original collection; it need not be the smallest possible choice.
subcover.rule: The selected sets must come from the given cover; replacing them with a newly invented covering set does not produce a subcover.
subcover.deep: Compactness requires a finite subcover for every open cover. The condition is stronger than the existence of one finite open cover: any subset of the real line is covered by the whole real line, but many subsets are not compact. The empty collection covers the empty set, so it is a finite subcover when the target is empty. These distinctions keep the quantifiers in compactness arguments precise.

subexponential_growth.label: subexponential growth
subexponential_growth.preview: Growth slower than every fixed exponential c^n with c>1.
subexponential_growth.card: Polynomial growth n¹⁰ is subexponential because n¹⁰/cⁿ→0 for every fixed c>1. The faster function exp(√n) is also subexponential, showing that subexponential does not mean polynomial or practically small.
subexponential_growth.rule: For positive sequences aₙ≥1, a standard equivalent condition is log(aₙ)/n→0. The comparison must hold against every fixed exponential base greater than one, rather than against just one especially large base.
subexponential_growth.deep: In the reciprocal-tail analysis, normalized vanishing can constrain denominator states to subexponential growth. That scale restriction then limits how frequently strict divisibility changes can occur, but it does not make the states bounded or convergent.

sublevel_set.label: sublevel set
sublevel_set.preview: A sublevel set of a real-valued function g at c is {x : g(x) ≤ c}; a strict sublevel set uses g(x) < c.
sublevel_set.card: The strict version is {x : g(x) < c}; the non-strict version is {x : g(x) ≤ c}. For a continuous function, these give an open and a closed set respectively.
sublevel_set.rule: Whether equality is allowed matters for paths and boundary points.
sublevel_set.deep: The Erdős #1041 material studies paths in the open region |p(z)| < 1. A path that only remains in the closed region |p(z)| ≤ 1 does not automatically meet that requirement.

subsequence.label: subsequence
subsequence.preview: A sequence formed by retaining terms at increasing indices.
subsequence.card: From 1,2,3,4,…, selecting indices 2,4,6,… produces the subsequence 2,4,6,…. Selecting square indices produces 1,4,9,16,…. Terms retain their original order although the gaps between chosen indices may grow.
subsequence.rule: A subsequence has form a_{n₁}, a_{n₂}, … with n₁ < n₂ < …. It need not be consecutive, but it preserves order. Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.
subsequence.deep: Sparse exceptional behavior may survive along a subsequence even when its proportion among all indices tends to zero. Consequently, typical or density-one estimates may be insufficient when a proof must exclude infinitely recurring exceptional denominator states.

subseries.label: subseries
subseries.preview: A subseries is formed by selecting terms from a series and keeping them in their original order.
subseries.card: For example, retaining only the even-indexed terms of ∑ aₙ gives a₂ + a₄ + a₆ + ⋯ . Its value, when defined, is a subsum of the original series.
subseries.rule: Selection differs from rearrangement: a rearrangement keeps all terms but changes their order.
subseries.deep: The Erdős #257 work asks about sums selected by infinite sets of exponents. The arithmetic pattern of the selected indices matters even when every such subseries converges.

subset.label: subset
subset.preview: A set A is a subset of B if every element of A also belongs to B.
subset.card: The notation A ⊆ B permits equality. For example, {2,4} is a subset of the even integers, and every set is a subset of itself. A proper subset excludes equality and therefore leaves at least one member of the larger set outside it.
subset.rule: The empty set is a subset of every set because it has no element that could violate the condition.
subset.deep: The papers use subsets to specify allowed indices, regions, and candidate families. Inclusion alone does not say that the subset is large, connected, dense, or representative of the larger set.

subsum.label: subsum
subsum.preview: A subsum is a sum obtained by retaining selected terms of a series and omitting the others.
subsum.card: If A is the selected index set, the expression is ∑ over n in A of aₙ. The resulting sequence of retained terms forms a subseries, whose sum must be defined when the selection is infinite.
subsum.rule: Convergence of the original series alone need not guarantee convergence of every subseries.
subsum.deep: For absolutely convergent series, every subseries converges. For nonnegative convergent series, subsums lie between zero and the full sum; their possible values can form an interesting set.

sum.label: sum
sum.preview: A sum is the result of adding quantities together.
sum.card: A finite sum adds a specified number of terms. An infinite series uses the limit of finite partial sums when that limit exists. The symbol ∑ abbreviates a sum with its index and range stated alongside it.
sum.rule: The range and order of summation can be part of the mathematical claim.
sum.deep: The papers distinguish exact finite arithmetic from conclusions about infinite sums. Passing from one to the other requires convergence and, when terms are rearranged, the appropriate justification for that rearrangement.

summability.label: summability
summability.preview: Summability means that a family of terms has a sum under a specified definition of infinite summation.
summability.card: For a nonnegative sequence, it means the partial sums are bounded and hence converge to a finite total. For real or complex families indexed without an order, the usual unconditional notion corresponds to absolute summability.
summability.rule: The terms, weighting, and summation convention are part of the claim.
summability.deep: In Lean, `Summable` has a formal meaning that should be checked for the relevant index and space. A convergent ordered series need not be summable in every stronger, order-independent sense.

superior_predictive_ability.label: superior predictive ability
superior_predictive_ability.preview: Hansen's superior predictive ability test assesses whether any candidate forecasting method has lower expected loss than a benchmark.
superior_predictive_ability.card: It compares a collection of methods jointly rather than treating the best observed performer as if it had been selected in advance. The procedure accounts for sampling variation and the comparison across candidates under its assumptions.
superior_predictive_ability.rule: The loss function, candidate set, dependence model, and resampling choices affect the inference.
superior_predictive_ability.deep: A rejection provides evidence against the benchmark's equal-or-better expected performance in the tested setting. It does not prove a particular method will outperform forever or explain why a difference occurs.

support.label: support
support.preview: Support can mean evidence for a claim or, in mathematics, the positions where a function or sequence is nonzero.
support.card: For a selected reciprocal sum, the papers also call the set of included indices its support. When terms are represented by zero-or-one selection coefficients, these two mathematical uses agree.
support.rule: The surrounding definition determines whether support refers to evidence, nonzero values, or selected indices.
support.deep: In analysis, the support of a function often means the closure of its nonzero set. That convention matters in topological settings and should not be silently substituted for an index set.

supremum.label: supremum
supremum.preview: The smallest number greater than or equal to every member of a set.
supremum.card: The open interval (0,1) has supremum 1 even though it has no largest member. Every element is at most 1, and any smaller proposed upper bound is exceeded by points sufficiently close to 1.
supremum.rule: A maximum must be attained; a supremum need not be. Unbounded-above sets may have supremum +∞ in the extended reals, and conventions for the empty set must be stated.
supremum.deep: The irrationality exponent is a supremum over approximation exponents achieved infinitely often. Calling it a supremum allows a sharp boundary value even when no single family of rational approximations attains that boundary exponent.

surjective_map.label: surjective map
surjective_map.preview: A function that attains every element of its stated codomain.
surjective_map.card: The map f(n)=n+1 from integers to integers is surjective because each target m has preimage m-1. The same formula from nonnegative integers to nonnegative integers is not surjective, since zero is never reached.
surjective_map.rule: Surjectivity depends on the stated codomain: every allowed target must have at least one input mapping to it. It says nothing about uniqueness of that input; uniqueness belongs to injectivity.
surjective_map.deep: The Lambert analysis proves certain coefficient maps are onto the integers, so every desired integer correction can be represented. Changing the domain, codomain, coefficient range, or degree bound can destroy that conclusion and must be tracked explicitly.

sylvester_sequence.label: Sylvester's sequence
sylvester_sequence.preview: Sylvester's sequence starts with 2, and each later term is one plus the product of all preceding terms.
sylvester_sequence.card: It begins 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807. With a₀ = 2, the same rule can be written aₙ₊₁ = aₙ(aₙ − 1) + 1, so each next term can be calculated directly from the previous one.
sylvester_sequence.rule: The starting value and indexing convention should be checked when comparing formulas.
sylvester_sequence.deep: Its terms are pairwise coprime and grow rapidly. Reciprocal identities associated with the sequence make it useful in questions about unit fractions and the values of structured infinite sums.

synth_seed.label: synth seed
synth_seed.preview: A synth seed is a concise, replaceable brief for the current phase of work.
synth_seed.card: It gathers the goal, reasons for the work, success conditions, relevant sources, and next planned activity. Plectis derives it from durable intent and current state so an agent can start without rereading all earlier material.
synth_seed.rule: It describes the current phase rather than preserving the operator's original words.
synth_seed.deep: As the work changes, the brief can be replaced while the underlying source and historical records remain. Its usefulness depends on staying aligned with the live objective and evidence.

synthetic.label: synthetic
synthetic.preview: Synthetic data is deliberately generated rather than directly observed from the real situation being studied.
synthetic.card: It may model typical inputs, isolate an edge case, or contain a known fault. Plectis uses synthetic fixtures to make particular checks repeatable and their expected outcomes explicit.
synthetic.rule: Generated data is useful when its relationship to the intended behaviour is clear.
synthetic.deep: A successful synthetic test establishes what happened under the constructed conditions. Extending that result to real use requires evidence that the relevant conditions and failure mechanisms have been represented adequately.

taylor_series.label: Taylor series
taylor_series.preview: A Taylor series is the power series whose coefficients are determined by a function’s derivatives at a chosen point.
taylor_series.card: For one variable, the coefficient of (x−c)ⁿ is f⁽ⁿ⁾(c)/n!. The exponential has Taylor series 1+x+x²/2!+… at zero. Its partial sums give polynomial approximations, with error controlled by a separate remainder estimate.
taylor_series.rule: Having derivatives of all orders does not ensure that the Taylor series converges or equals the function. Analyticity supplies local equality.
taylor_series.deep: For example, exp(−1/x²), extended by zero at x = 0, is smooth and has every derivative zero there, yet it is positive elsewhere. Its Taylor series at zero therefore misses those values. Finite Taylor approximations and infinite series equality make different claims.

telemetry.label: telemetry
